name: Fortran (gfortran) in niklas-heer/speed-comparison: Leibniz pi series
baseline: C (gcc 15.2.0, -O3 -flto -march=native with -fno-signed-zeros -fno-trapping-math -fassociative-math) and the clang / C++ builds of the same Leibniz loop in the same suite
workload: Single-threaded Leibniz series for pi, 1,000,000,000 terms per run, three recorded runs per target (TimesPerRun in the raw JSON), median wall time.
claimed_speedup: Published snapshot 2026-09-05T193245, combined_results.csv medians in ms: Fortran 90 (gfortran 14.3.0) 141.67 vs C (gcc 15.2.0) 157.9, about 1.11x (derived from page data); vs C++ (g++) 158.78, about 1.12x (derived); vs C (clang 21.1.2) 146.07, about 1.03x (derived); vs C++ (clang++) 143.32, about 1.01x (derived). Min-max ranges: Fortran 141.04-144.35 ms, C++ clang++ 142.74-144.96 ms, C (clang) 143.63-150.61 ms, C (gcc) 155.46-160.78 ms, so the lead over the clang builds is inside the sample range.
compiler_and_flags: Fortran: gfortran 14.3.0 `gfortran leibniz.f90 -o leibniz -Ofast -flto -ffast-math -march=native -mtune=native`. C: gcc 15.2.0 `gcc -O3 -s -flto -march=native -mtune=native -fomit-frame-pointer -fno-signed-zeros -fno-trapping-math -fassociative-math -o leibniz leibniz.c -lm`. C++ clang++ 21.1.2 and C clang 21.1.2 use the same flag set (from docs/history/2026-09-05T193245/raw/*.json).
hardware: AMD EPYC-Genoa Processor, 4 threads, shared x86-64 VM (runner homelab-argo), kernel 6.18.38-talos
tradeoffs: The suite compares single implementations of one arithmetic loop, not Fortran as a whole. The Fortran loop is written differently from the C loop: it is unrolled by hand to four terms per iteration (src/leibniz.f90), while C/C++ use a one-term loop with an `i & 1` sign trick written to allow vectorisation (src/leibniz.c).
caveats: Evidence would qualify as A (code, compiler versions, flags and CPU model are all public) but the source states no mechanism, so the tier is capped at C. The margin over the best C/C++ build (clang++ 143.32 ms) is about 1% and inside the three-sample ranges; the suite's own README warns that three samples cannot establish a winner for small differences. Flags are not matched: gfortran is built with -Ofast (includes -ffast-math and -freciprocal-math) while C sets only -fno-signed-zeros -fno-trapping-math -fassociative-math, and the compiler versions differ (gfortran 14.3.0 vs gcc 15.2.0). The suite's accuracy column shows 9.440 correct digits for Fortran vs 9.499 for C and a 12-digit printout for Fortran, consistent with different arithmetic (not verified). Nim (142.43 ms) and Rust SIMD (141.31 ms) are also faster than gcc C in the same snapshot; Nim compiles through gcc, so that gap comes from source form, not language. Explicit-SIMD C++ (AVX2) is slower (290.67 ms). In the earlier snapshot docs/history/2025-12-14T070941 (gfortran 14.2.0) Fortran took 238.94 ms: about 1.06x faster than C (gcc) 253.23 ms (derived from page data) but slower than C++ (clang++) 223.89 ms and level with C (clang) 237.46 ms, so only the lead over gcc-built C is repeatable. The HEAD pipeline/languages.py pins different compiler versions than the snapshot; the snapshot's per-target JSON was used here.

name: ClangJIT (Clang with JIT extensions for C++ templates)
baseline: Ahead-of-time compiled Eigen benchmark (adapted bench/benchmark.cpp) using runtime-sized dynamic matrices, built with the same Clang at -O3 -march=native -ffast-math
workload: Eigen bench/benchmark.cpp adapted: 40,000,000 repeats of small dense matrix operations; AoT runtime-sized matrices versus JIT-instantiated fixed-size matrices for sizes 3, 7 and 16, JIT compile time excluded from the runtime rows.
claimed_speedup: Runtime, 40M repeats, JIT compile time excluded: size 3 JIT 1.0s vs AoT 8.05s; size 7 JIT 8.34s vs AoT 20s; size 16 JIT 35.3s vs AoT 36.2s (about 8x, 2.4x and 1.03x, derived from page data). Compile time (user): JIT build 3.5s total vs AoT double-only 5.3s and AoT three-float-types-with-dispatch 9.7s.
compiler_and_flags: ClangJIT (Clang fork, -fjit, [[clang::jit]] attribute) with -march=native -ffast-math -O3 as stated in the wiki table header; Clang itself built with GCC 8.2.0
hardware: Xeon E5-2699 (exact variant not stated)
tradeoffs: Needs a custom Clang/LLVM fork (not upstream); the program links the compiler infrastructure and compiles templates at run time (JIT start-up cost, memory, requires source or serialized AST available at run time); restrictions on decltype(auto), explicit specializations and pointer arguments listed on the wiki; the WG21 proposal P1609 for [[jit]] has not been adopted.
caveats: The AoT baseline is Eigen with dynamic (runtime-sized) matrices; the wiki's 'single specialization' column (1.01s, 8.45s, 35.1s) shows an AoT build specialized for one known size matches the JIT run time, so the win is over generic AoT code, not over size-specialized AoT code. Win shrinks to 1.03x at size 16. Wiki is first-party and numbers are single runs (no variance given). The paper (arXiv 1904.08555, SC19 P3HPC workshop) could not be opened (arxiv.org blocked), so only the wiki was checked. Whether the JIT'd code gets exactly the same -O3 level as the AoT code is assumed from the wiki's flag header. Repository last commit is Dec 2019.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Clang-JIT C++ template instantiation at runtime speedup over ahead-of-time compiled code paper github' surfaced arXiv 1904.08555 and P1609; repo wiki then opened on github.com.
why_faster: Runtime values (matrix dimensions) become template arguments instantiated at run time, so the optimizer sees fixed sizes and can unroll and vectorize; only the sizes actually used are compiled (wiki: 'performance benefits of many AoT specializations, sometimes better, at a low compile-time cost').

name: HotSpot Java Math.sin/% loop vs C libm sin/fmod at gcc -O3: xemantic/java-2-times-faster-than-c
baseline: C loop calling libm sin() and fmod() (src/main/c/almost_pseudo_random.c) built with gcc -O3 -lm; the README's 'Clang' row again comes from a gcc build
workload: Sum fmod(sin(i * 100000.0) + 1.0, 1.0) for 1,000,000,000 iterations (a trigonometry-based pseudo-random function from The Book of Shaders).
claimed_speedup: Java 51.235 s vs GCC C 1 m 4.433 s and 'Clang' C 1 m 4.878 s (real time, one run each): about 1.26x faster than gcc C (derived from page data). Contributed Go finished in 28.191 s (faster than both), Rust in 1 m 7.944 s.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc -O3 -lm with no -ffast-math (build-gcc.sh); compiler and glibc versions not stated. Java: Gradle build with source level 15, default JVM flags.
hardware: Intel Core i7-8550U @ 1.80GHz (4 cores, 8 threads), about 16 GB RAM (README /proc/cpuinfo dump)
why_faster: Author cannot fully explain it and lists hypotheses: HotSpot inlines aggressively after profiling, C math functions come from a library and cannot be inlined, and Java's % operator on doubles may map to better machine code.
tradeoffs: Measures the speed of the runtime's sin and floating-point remainder implementation against glibc's, not general code generation; JVM start-up and memory not compared.
caveats: One run per implementation (shell 'time'); compiler, glibc and JDK versions not stated, and gcc without -ffast-math or -fno-math-errno keeps libm calls for sin and fmod. The Java checksum prints as 4.9999999712235045E8 against 499999997.122350 for C (same value to the printed digits). Go, with slightly different floating-point results, was 2x faster than both, so the gap measures math-library cost rather than a language-level code-generation win.

name: HotSpot Java ring-of-nodes mutation vs C at gcc -O3: xemantic/java-2-times-faster-than-c
baseline: C ring-of-nodes program (src/main/c/java_2_times_faster_than_c.c, malloc and free per node and per payload) built with gcc -O3; the README's 'Clang' row comes from build-clang.sh, which actually invokes gcc
workload: Build a ring of 10,000 nodes with a pseudo-random payload of 0-49 bytes, then run 1,000,000 mutations that each delete and insert up to 200 nodes; node count and checksum are identical in every implementation.
claimed_speedup: Java (HotSpot) 8.569 s vs GCC C 12.800 s and 'Clang' C 12.726 s (real time, one run each): about 1.5x faster than C (derived from page data). The project title claims 2x and the README dialogue says 'almost 2 times faster'; the measured ratio is about 1.5x.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc -O3 -lm (build-gcc.sh); build-clang.sh also calls gcc -O3, not clang; compiler and glibc versions not stated. Java: Gradle build with source and target level 15, run as java -cp build/classes/java/main with default JVM flags (JDK build not stated).
hardware: Intel Core i7-8550U @ 1.80GHz (4 cores, 8 threads), about 16 GB RAM (README /proc/cpuinfo dump)
why_faster: Author's hypothesis: certain algorithms gain performance just from being expressed with automatic memory management, because the C version pays a malloc and a free per node and per payload while the JVM allocates and reclaims in bulk. The README adds that better memory management in C (issue #1) can beat the Java version.
tradeoffs: JVM needs a runtime and has higher memory use (not measured in the README). The C version could be sped up with a pool or arena allocator, which the author deliberately did not add.
caveats: One run per implementation measured with the shell 'time' (no variance). Compiler and JDK versions are not stated, and the 'Clang' row was built with gcc by build-clang.sh. Every new node and every mutation count calls sin() and fmod() through libm, so part of the gap is the libm cost shown in the second benchmark of the same repo (Java 51.2 s vs C 64.4 s for 1e9 calls). The author calls the title provocative, says it applies only to this algorithm, and notes that explicit memory management in C beats the Java version. Contributed Rust (13.824 s) and Go (14.542 s) were slower than C, C# (34.037 s) much slower.

compiler_and_flags: C/C++: Clang 22.1.8 and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk). Headline 'prod' build is -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer (not -O3). The same suite also builds 'Fast' (-O3 -march=native -mtune=native -funroll-loops, thin LTO), 'Unsafe' (-O3 -march=native -ffast-math, full LTO) and 'PGO' (-O2 plus profile) variants of every C and C++ benchmark; all 16 Clang/GCC x C/C++ configurations were compared here. why_faster: The suite's own docs/ai_analysis.js says Julia specializes sort! on Int32 at run time and picks a radix or counting sort (O(n)), and docs/ai_critic.js says this is the standard library choosing a better algorithm for the data type, not the language being faster ('You're comparing algorithms, not languages').

name: NonuniformFFTs.jl (Julia NUFFT, CPU and GPU) vs FINUFFT and cuFINUFFT
baseline: FINUFFT v2.4.1 (C++, CPU) and cuFINUFFT (CUDA C++, GPU), both compiled locally and called through FINUFFT.jl v3.4.0
workload: Type-1 and type-2 3D non-uniform FFTs on a uniform 256^3 grid, random points in [0, 2*pi)^3 with point density N/M^3 from 1e-4 to 10, tolerance 1e-6, Float64 complex data; each time includes set_points plus the transform.
claimed_speedup: README: on CPU 'comparable performance' to FINUFFT (no CPU win claimed); on GPU it 'can be faster than the CUDA-based CuFINUFFT, especially for large problem sizes'. Docs: the default global-memory GPU method is 'slightly faster than CuFINUFFT at low point densities, but slightly slower at large ones'; the non-default shared-memory method gives 'important gains with respect to the CuFINUFFT implementation' at large densities. The gains appear only in plots; no numeric ratio is printed on either page.
compiler_and_flags: FINUFFT built with Nvidia nvc++ via CMake 'Release' with default flags (FFTW.ESTIMATE, spread_sort=1, spread_kerevalmeth=1, tolerance 1e-6, modeord=1); cuFINUFFT built with nvcc from CUDA 12.8 and CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=90; NonuniformFFTs.jl v0.8.3 (2025-07-11) on Julia with KernelAbstractions.jl/CUDA.jl (Julia version not stated on the page). Script: benchmark/CPU+CUDA/run_benchmarks.jl.
hardware: Jean Zay (IDRIS): 2x Intel Xeon Platinum 8468 (24 cores used) and one NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80 GB (1/4 of a node). A second run on one AMD Instinct MI300A (Adastra) compares only the CPU against FINUFFT.
why_faster: Docs, GPU only and hedged: the shared-memory variant 'completely avoids atomic operations on shared memory', which 'seems to speed up things quite a bit and might explain the important gains' over cuFINUFFT. The implementation is described as 'heavily inspired' by the cuFINUFFT paper, so the algorithm family is the same but not identical.
tradeoffs: Julia package; one KernelAbstractions.jl code base targets CUDA, AMD and other GPUs. Also offers real-valued non-uniform data transforms (extra gains, not available in FINUFFT).
caveats: Author's own benchmark, results only as SVG plots with no numeric table. The CPU result is parity, not a win. The GPU win is regime dependent: the default method is slower than cuFINUFFT at high density and the faster shared-memory method has to be chosen. The 'real data' gains solve a different (real-valued) problem. On AMD GPUs the default method scales badly. Only one GPU model (H100) and one tolerance (1e-6) were tested, and the Julia compiler version is not stated.

name: OCaml 5.4.1: benchLANG binary trees vs C and C++ at -O3
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off) and C++ (g++ -std=c++20 with the same flags) binary-trees programs that allocate every node with malloc/free (C) or new/delete (C++)
workload: CLBG-style binary trees, depths 4 to 18: allocate, traverse and (in native code) free complete binary trees of individually allocated nodes; the README says the workload measures allocator plus GC plus pointer chasing, with native frees inside the timer and GC runtimes collecting when they like.
claimed_speedup: OCaml 5.4.1 0.865 s vs C 1.010 s and C++ 1.147 s: about 1.17x faster than C and 1.33x faster than C++ (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 16.2.0 -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s; C++: g++ 16.2.0 -std=c++20 with the same flags (nixpkgs-unstable pins). OCaml: ocamlopt -O3 -unsafe -inline 200 -nodynlink monotonic.c (-O3 only has an effect when the compiler was built with flambda; the nixpkgs build's flambda status is not stated).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz (cpupower performance governor, min and max 3500 MHz), 48 GB DDR4-3600 CL16, Arch Linux
why_faster: Source (README workload note): native code frees every node inside the timed region while GC runtimes collect when they like. Likely mechanism (inference): bump-pointer allocation in the runtime and deferred or concurrent reclamation against glibc malloc and free per node.
tradeoffs: Whole-process peak RSS 89.7 MiB for OCaml vs 33.3 MiB for C; OCaml is slower than C on primes (3.200 s vs 2.725 s), Fibonacci (4.897 s vs 1.694 s) and strings (5.000 s vs 2.132 s).
caveats: One run per language (no variance) from a single machine on 2026-09-03. The C and C++ programs are naive per-node malloc/free; an arena or pool allocator in C would beat the runtimes here. The benchmark is 1 of 5 workloads, and C wins overall (total 9.762 s vs Java 13.536 s, C# 11.914 s, OCaml 16.233 s; C is faster on Fibonacci, strings and, for Java and OCaml, primes). Managed runtimes keep default settings with JIT warm-up inside the timed region and may use extra GC and JIT threads, so wall time is not CPU time. OCaml's win is modest (1.17x) and rests on a single run; the bump allocation of the minor heap is why the allocation-heavy test favours it, not general code quality.

name: Julia (no BLAS) matmul with @fastmath @simd ivdep in kostya/benchmarks
baseline: C/gcc matmul (matmul/matmul.c): transposed-B dot-product triple loop on double**, gcc -O3 -march=native -flto, no -ffast-math
workload: 1500x1500 double matrix multiply (MSIZE 1500) written as plain loops (no BLAS) in each language.
claimed_speedup: Matmul: Julia (no BLAS) 1.113s vs C/gcc 3.034s and C/clang 3.067s (about 2.7x, derived from page data). BLAS-backed rows (Eigen 0.081s, Julia threads:1 0.17s) are a different algorithm class and not the claim.
compiler_and_flags: C++ baseline: g++ 16.1.0 -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -std=c++23 (common/commands.mk); clang++ 22.1.8 row also present; runtimes: .NET 10.0.100, Scala 3.8.4, Racket 9.2
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2324G (README Environment section); Debian forky/sid Docker image

caveats: Not an equal-optimization comparison: the Julia loop uses @fastmath and @simd ivdep (permits FP reassociation, vectorization) and an axpy loop order (c[m,n] += a[m,k]*b[k,n]), while the C baseline is a strict-FP dot-product loop built without -ffast-math or restrict, which gcc -O3 cannot vectorize. A C build with -ffast-math (or the same loop order) would likely close most of the gap. The Julia file also uses Threads.@threads, and the thread count used for this row is not stated on the README page. Capped at C for the mismatched optimization level.

why_faster: Per-statement fast-math and ivdep annotations allow the LLVM vectorizer to reassociate and vectorize the inner loop that strict-FP gcc -O3 does not (derived from reading matmul/matmul.jl and matmul.c; not stated in the README).

The author notes a faster C++ program is possible. No licence file, so the code is reference only. gcc 4.9.1-era results, CPU model not stated, single timing per language.

name: LuaJIT 2.0 FFI: dyu/ffi-overhead plusone() call loop
baseline: C and C++ (gcc 5.4.1 -O2) calling plusone() in the shared library libnewplus.so through the dynamic linker
workload: Call the C function plusone(int) in a loop 500,000,000 times (while (x < count) x = plusone(x)) and report elapsed milliseconds.
claimed_speedup: LuaJIT 891 ms and 905 ms vs C 1182 ms and 1182 ms (C++ 1182 and 1183 ms) for 500M calls: about 1.3x faster (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: C and C++: gcc/g++ 5.4.1 -O2 -fPIC (Tuprules.tup), executable linked against newplus/libnewplus.so; luajit 2.0.4; julia 0.6.3; Ubuntu 14.04; 2 samples per language.
hardware: Intel i7-3630QM laptop (4 cores, HT), 16 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Gain only applies to call-boundary overhead for very small functions.
caveats: Measures foreign-call overhead for a trivial function, not code quality. The C and C++ rows call through the PLT of a shared library, which the FFI/ccall code of the JIT languages avoids; statically linking or LTO-inlining plusone in C would remove the call entirely (agent inference from the Tupfile; the README itself states no mechanism, so the tier is capped at C; an HN search snippet reported a commenter attributing a LuaJIT-over-C result to direct calls versus PLT calls, but it did not name this repo). C is compiled -O2, not -O3. Toolchains are from 2018 (julia 0.6.3, luajit 2.0.4, gcc 5.4.1) and only 2 samples are shown. Many other languages in the table are slower than C (Go 37,975 ms, Node 9,163 ms, Java 4,469 ms).

name: NativeMinuit.jl (pure-Julia port of C++ Minuit2)
baseline: C++ Minuit2 (ROOT's standalone Minuit2 built through CMake, default Release, C++17) running MIGRAD on the same objectives

claimed_speedup: Julia/C++ time ratios 0.147x (quad_4d: 0.81 us vs 5.50 us), 0.253x (rosenbrock_2d: 9.50 vs 37.62 us), 0.371x (rosenbrock_10d: 58.11 vs 156.62 us), 0.718x (gauss_ll_10_1000: 32.26 vs 44.96 us), 0.888x (gauss_ll_2_100: 20.16 vs 22.71 us): about 1.1x to 6.8x faster (derived from page data). README: 'Faster than C++ Minuit2 on every benchmark in the test corpus'.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.12 with OpenBLAS 0.3.29, single-threaded BLAS on both sides; C++ side built with benchmark/cpp/CMakeLists.txt (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE defaults to Release, C++17); C++ compiler and exact flags not stated.
hardware: Apple M3
why_faster: Stated by the README: a parametric CostFunction{F} devirtualizes the FCN call site at compile time, whereas C++ Minuit2 pays for shared_ptr ref-counting and ABObj expression-template dispatch.
stars_or_usage: 14 stars; registered in the Julia General registry
tradeoffs: Needs the Julia runtime and JIT warm-up (the README table does not say whether compile time is excluded); a derivative work of Minuit2, so LGPL applies; not a drop-in for C++ callers.
caveats: First-party numbers from the port's author, microsecond-scale runs on toy objectives of 2 to 10 parameters where call and dispatch overhead dominate; the C++ compiler and flags are not stated, and the C++ Minuit2 tree the CMake file expects at reference/Minuit2_cpp is not in the repository listing, so the C++ version is unspecified. The port reimplements the algorithm; the README says its algorithms were 'audited against C++ Minuit2', but the page shows no equal iteration or function-call counts. The stated mechanism (call-site devirtualization) suggests the gain is dispatch and inlining of the user function rather than the numerical core.

name: OrdinaryDiffEq.jl (DifferentialEquations.jl) ODE solvers vs Sundials, ODEPACK and Hairer codes
baseline: Sundials CVODE_Adams and ARKODE (C), ODEPACK lsoda (Fortran) and Hairer dopri5/dop853/odex (Fortran), called through Julia wrappers
workload: Work-precision diagrams (wall time versus error at tolerances 1e-6 to 1e-13) for non-stiff ODEs: Lotka-Volterra, Pleiades and Three-Body.
claimed_speedup: No numbers on the pages (plots only). Text: 'Here we see the OrdinaryDiffEq.jl algorithms once again far in the lead' (LotkaVolterra_wpd.md); 'The OrdinaryDiffEq.jl algorithms come out as faster in each case than the ODEInterface algorithms' (Pleiades_wpd.md). SciMLBenchmarks.jl README: ARKODE and Hairer dopri5/dop853 'both far less efficient than the Vern methods'; CVODE_Adams and lsoda 'tend to not do very well'.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.11.9 (LLVM 16.0.6 ORCJIT, znver2); the C and Fortran baselines come from prebuilt JLL binaries and their build flags are not on the pages
hardware: 128 x AMD EPYC 7502 32-Core Processor (SciML CI runner)
tradeoffs: Julia JIT start-up and package precompilation; wins depend on the Verner high-order Runge-Kutta methods and algorithm-specific interpolation that the C and Fortran codes do not provide.
caveats: First-party benchmark (the SciML authors wrote both sides' harness); results are plots, so no speedup number can be quoted from the page. The compared solvers use different algorithms (Verner/Tsit5 RK vs Adams/BDF/Dormand-Prince), so this is partly an algorithm win; wrapped C/Fortran codes are called through Julia with their own callback overhead into the Julia ODE function, which may penalize the baselines. Sundials and ODEPACK are not built from source with stated -O3 flags. Some timing differences on easy problems are described by the benchmark itself as dominated by start-up time.

name: pflua (pflang packet-filter compiler on LuaJIT) vs libpcap BPF interpreter and Linux kernel BPF JITs
baseline: libpcap user-space BPF interpreter (C); also the old 2011 Linux kernel BPF JIT and the 2014 Linux eBPF JIT (C), both adapted to run in user space by the pflua-bench repo
workload: Run pflang (tcpdump filter language) expressions such as 'accept all', 'ip', 'tcp', 'tcp port 5555' and 'icmp' over a saved capture of about 1M ICMP ping packets, measured in millions of packets per second (MPPS), 50 runs per implementation in one process after a discarded warm-up run.
claimed_speedup: README: 'In many circumstances, pflua is the fastest pflang implementation out there, by a long shot.' Medians of the 20 runs in results/ping-flood (derived from page data), MPPS pflua vs libpcap vs linux-bpf vs linux-ebpf: 'tcp' 89.9 vs 37.9 vs 62.2 vs 56.1; 'tcp port 5555' 89.9 vs 37.9 vs 61.8 vs 57.6; 'icmp' 89.9 vs 54.8 vs 83.5 vs 77.7; 'ip' 91.6 vs 68.0 vs 85.3 vs 78.7; 'accept all' 127.9 vs 92.1 vs 109.8 vs 95.4. That is about 2.4x libpcap and 1.4x the Linux 2011 BPF JIT on the 'tcp' filter.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. pflua embeds LuaJIT (built with make); the libpcap and Linux BPF/eBPF JIT C code are built with make in pflua-bench with no flags given in the README.
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 (x86-64), Debian GNU/Linux (3.14-2), otherwise unloaded machine (pflua-bench README)
why_faster: Source (pflua README, Performance section): LuaJIT trace compilation emits machine code specialised to the traffic actually seen; pflua can hoist and eliminate bounds checks while BPF must check every packet access; it works in network byte order while BPF converts to host order; it uses LuaJIT's register allocator and optimizer whereas the Linux kernel JIT has a limited optimizer.
stars_or_usage: 312 stars (pflua); 26 stars (pflua-bench); written for the Snabb user-space networking toolkit
tradeoffs: Needs LuaJIT; filters are compiled at run time and the speed depends on LuaJIT trace behaviour; pflua is a filter engine only, not a full libpcap replacement, and the project says there may be bugs or differences against libpcap.
caveats: First-party benchmark by the pflua authors with the compiler flags of the C baselines unstated, so tier C. The compared pflang pipelines use different algorithms (pflua has its own optimizer; libpcap runs an unoptimised BPF interpreter), so this is partly an optimiser win. The README text says about 180 MPPS for the ping flood while the CSV medians show 128 MPPS for 'accept all' and about 90 MPPS for tcp/icmp, so the prose and the raw CSVs do not match exactly. On the real-world wingolog.org capture pflua is sometimes slower than libpcap and the Linux JITs, which the authors blame on LuaJIT trace state-transfer costs. The README notes the ping-flood filters can run faster than the 'accept all' loop, so the harness overhead is not fully separated. Last commit 2017 (pflua) and 2016 (pflua-bench), so numbers are about nine years old.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github LuaJIT OR Java OR JVM outperforms C DPDK OR C implementation packet processing OR database OR codec benchmark JIT faster' led to Igalia/pflua; opened the pflua README, the pflua-bench README and results/ping-flood CSVs (libpcap.csv, linux-bpf.csv, linux-ebpf.csv, pflua.csv)

name: SymbolicUtils.jl / Symbolics.jl (Julia symbolic engine) vs SymEngine (C++): SciMLBenchmarks SymEngineComparison

workload: Ten symbolic workloads adapted from SymEngine's own C++ benchmark suite plus SymbolicUtils-native ones: diff of expand((x^y+y^z+z^x)^50), 15-term Taylor series, trig-product substitution, 10^5-draw random-expression substitution (dense and sparse rule), variable search on shared and unshared expression sets, numeric evaluation of a 10000-deep expression, code-generation init, and the call of the generated function with common-subexpression elimination.
claimed_speedup: SymbolicUtils is faster than SymEngine in 4 of 10 rows (SymEngine s vs SymbolicUtils s): compiled call with CSE 6.93256e-7 vs 3.13135e-7 (2.2x), variable search on dissimilar expressions 4.67036e-4 vs 2.13078e-4 (2.2x), variable search on common subtrees 1.02663e-3 vs 4.89876e-4 (2.1x), substitution of a 10^5-draw expression with a sparse rule 1.10077e-3 vs 5.92595e-4 (1.9x) (ratios derived from page data). SymEngine is faster in the other 6: diff of expand 6.95691e-3 vs 0.332787 (SymbolicUtils 48x slower), eval_double of a 10000-deep expression 0.0116745 vs 0.331982 (28x), codegen init 1.15092e-3 vs 1.34645e-2 (12x), series 1.99123e-3 vs 1.98982e-2 (10x), trig-product substitution 1.478e-5 vs 6.0009e-5 (4.1x), dense-rule substitution 1.13195e-3 vs 3.95472e-3 (3.5x).
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.13.0 (LLVM 20.1.8, znver2), SymbolicUtils v4.46.6, Symbolics v7.39.2, SymEngine.jl v0.13.2 with the prebuilt SymEngine_jll v0.12.0+0 binary (its compiler and flags are not stated); timings are minimum over samples (Chairmarks). Source: SciML/SciMLBenchmarks.jl benchmarks/Symbolics/SymEngineComparison.jmd.
hardware: 128 x AMD EPYC 7502 32-Core Processor (128 virtual cores), Linux x86_64 CI runner
why_faster: Per the benchmark text: the substitution and search wins use SymbolicUtils' IRStructure acceleration structure, which visits shared subexpressions once; the compiled-call win is a native Julia function produced by Code.toexpr plus eval (JIT compiled), against SymEngine's LambdaRealDoubleVisitor, which the file describes as 'an interpreter over the expression tree'.
tradeoffs: The JIT path pays a large setup cost: codegen init is 12x slower than SymEngine's. Core operations (expand, differentiate, series, deep evaluation) are 10-48x slower than SymEngine in this run.
caveats: First-party benchmark by the Symbolics/SciML maintainers, single run without variance. The file itself says the first workload set 'plays to SymEngine's strengths' and the second set is SymbolicUtils-native; for substitution and search rows the SymbolicUtils column is the faster of two variants (plain and IRStructure-backed). The SymEngine 'variable search' is free_symbols accumulation into a set, not an identical operation. The compiled-call row excludes the 12x higher compile cost. The C++ build flags of SymEngine_jll are not stated, so the baseline's optimisation level is unknown.

Independent corroboration: in LangArena CSV::Parse (2026-10-05) the Zig row, which imports csv-zero, takes 0.974 s vs 2.223 s for the best C row (C/Clang) and 2.348 s for C++/Clang++.
compiler_and_flags: csv-race Makefile: Zig 'zig build --release=fast' (README names Zig 0.15.2); zsv 'cc -O3 main.c -lzsv' (libzsv's own build flags not stated); lazycsv 'g++ -std=c++17 -O3 -march=native'; Rust 'cargo build --release'. Timed with poop (perf counters) or hyperfine.

why_faster: README of csv-zero: SIMD-accelerated scanning, a zero-allocation field iterator that returns slices into one internal buffer, and strict RFC 4180 validation that simplifies fast paths. The author's blog post with details (peymanmo.com) was not opened (host blocked).
stars_or_usage: 38 stars (csv-zero); companion harness csv-race has 2 stars

Single machine (laptop-class Ryzen 5 PRO 5650U), one table. Compile-time summary goes the other way: pcre2 1.41, pcre2/jit 6.20, rust/regex 11.85, re2 12.28. LangArena results 2026-10-05, Etc::LogParser: Rust 0.302 s vs C with PCRE2 JIT 0.485 s (clang) and 0.488 s (gcc), about 1.6x, and vs C++ 0.99 s. why_faster: Not stated by the suite. Code reading (rust/src/benchmarks/compress.rs, c/src/compress.c, cpp/src/compress.cpp): all three use prefix doubling over rank pairs, but the sorting step differs: Rust calls the standard library's stable sort_by, C runs two counting-sort passes with fresh malloc/calloc buffers per step, C++ calls std::sort. caveats: The three implementations use different sort strategies, so same_algorithm is false; a periodic input is close to a best case for an adaptive sort. name: A*PA2 (astar-pairwise-aligner)
baseline: Edlib (C++) and BiWFA / WFA2-lib (C) exact global aligners
workload: Exact global pairwise alignment (edit distance) of long DNA sequences, e.g. ONT reads of a human genome with 6% to 11% divergence, plus synthetic sequences.
claimed_speedup: Repo README: 'up to 20x speedup over other exact aligners and is competitive with approximate aligners'. Paper abstract as quoted in a WebSearch snippet (WABI 2024, LIPIcs 312, paper page blocked): 19x faster than BiWFA and Edlib on >500 kbp ONT reads at 6% divergence; 5.6x at 11 kbp reads with 11% divergence; 0.81x (slower) on 800 bp reads at 11% divergence; A*PA2-simple is 6x to 8x faster than Edlib for sequences of at least 10 kbp.
why_faster: Per the paper snippet: like Edlib it uses Ukkonen band doubling with Myers bit-packing, adding large blocks, SIMD, a new profile and the A* heuristics from A*PA (a different algorithm, not a language effect).
tradeoffs: Gains only on long, low-divergence inputs; slower than Edlib on short, highly divergent reads. Latest commit message mentions 'latest nightly', so a nightly Rust toolchain may be needed (not confirmed). MPL-2.0 is file-level copyleft. Evaluation harness lives in a separate pa-bench repo.
caveats: Only the 'up to 20x' README sentence was verified on a page I opened; the 19x, 5.6x and 0.81x figures are snippet only from the peer-reviewed paper. CPU and flags not found. Pairwise alignment is on the edge of the string-and-text category.
found_via: WebSearch 'A*PA2 exact global sequence alignment Rust faster than Edlib WFA github astarpa2'; opened the repo page and commits feed.

name: Sassy (SIMD approximate string matching)
baseline: Edlib (C++ Myers bit-vector aligner); parasail (C) and SWOffinder also compared in the paper
workload: Searching short DNA/ASCII patterns (up to about 1000 characters) in long texts allowing k edit errors, synthetic data and a human genome search.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract as returned in a WebSearch snippet (the bioRxiv page itself is blocked here): 4x to 15x faster than Edlib for patterns up to 1000 bp, text throughput near 2 Gbp/s, over 100x faster than parasail, 100x faster than SWOffinder on CRISPR off-target search. Repo README: version 2 is 2x faster on AVX-512 and pre-encoding patterns is 10-20x faster for short texts (these are internal comparisons).
compiler_and_flags: README: build with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' (AVX2 or NEON needed); Edlib build flags not seen.
why_faster: Bit-packing with SIMD (AVX2/NEON) where the bit-vectors run along the text direction ('tiling in the text direction'), with the text split into 4 parts searched in parallel; complexity O(k ceil(n/W)) with W=256.
stars_or_usage: 169 stars; published on crates.io, bioconda and PyPI (sassy-rs)
tradeoffs: Needs AVX2 or NEON; supports ASCII, DNA and IUPAC alphabets; best for patterns up to about 1000; C bindings, Python bindings and a CLI exist.
caveats: Numbers come from the paper abstract as quoted in a search snippet (snippet only); the preprint, the Bioinformatics article (doi 10.1093/bioinformatics/btag244, listed on the README) and the eval CSVs were not opened. Edlib uses no explicit SIMD, so the comparison pits AVX2 against a scalar-word Myers implementation. The README itself never states the Edlib ratio. Repository evals/ directory has the harness (run_tool_bench.py) so a reproduction is possible.

baseline: mawk 1.3.4 and GNU gawk 5.4.0 (C); BSD awk on macOS also timed
workload: hyperfine on 1,000,000-line inputs: '{ print $1 }', sum of first column, multi-field print, regex filter, associative-array count, conditional field print, field arithmetic, string concatenation, no-match gsub, plus a CPU-bound BEGIN loop.
claimed_speedup: README tables (mean ms, awkrs vs mawk vs gawk): { print $1 } 15.7 vs 66.2 vs 100.8; sum first column 13.0 vs 37.5 vs 62.9; multi-field print 56.4 vs 156.6 vs 266.1; regex filter 11.1 vs 19.3 vs 351.4; associative array 340.0 vs 610.0 vs 342.4 (parity with gawk); NR%2 field print 30.2 vs 71.1 vs 116.1; field computation 19.0 vs 57.7 vs 100.5; string concat print 51.0 vs 121.0 vs 182.2; CPU-bound BEGIN loop 9.2 vs 9.7 vs 20.7.

caveats: First-party, single machine (macOS arm64), whose mawk/gawk are probably distribution builds; the fast paths read regular files through mmap and skip the VM, while the baselines read through their general record loop; the README's own 2026-06-01 caveat says the JIT rows come from a Cranelift module that has since been removed. name: cuniq (Rust unique-line counter)
baseline: GNU coreutils 8.32 `sort -u | wc -l` and `sort | uniq -c`, and GNU awk 5.3.2 (`a[$0]++`), all C programs.
workload: Count distinct lines (and per-line occurrence counts) of a 32 GiB preprocessed Wikipedia text dump with 6,028,206,370 lines, 78,035,032 of them unique; also a 4,000,000-line random-number file in criterion benches.
claimed_speedup: PERFORMANCE.md, 32 GiB test: `sort -u huge.txt | wc -l` 14m11.935s vs `cuniq --memmap --threads=1` 2m47.462s (5.1x, derived from page data), `cuniq --memmap --mode=near-exact` (16 threads) 59.387 s (14.3x, derived), `--mode=estimate` (HyperLogLog, 0.74% error) 9.038 s. Report mode: `sort | uniq -c` 28m46.811s and awk 25m03.082s vs `cuniq --memmap -c` 3m07.817s (9.2x and 8.0x, derived). README: 'For counting cuniq reliably outperforms GNU sort in all cases', with one exception for reports on inputs with almost no duplicates.
compiler_and_flags: Rust nightly with `RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" cargo +nightly build -Z build-std=std --target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` (recipe in PERFORMANCE.md, with profile-guided optimization mentioned); GNU tools are prebuilt Windows binaries run from Git Bash, build flags unknown.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D (16 threads), 5200 MT/s memory, 6950 MB/s sequential disk read, Windows 11 24H2
why_faster: PERFORMANCE.md optimization list: hash table instead of sorting (O(n)), memory-mapped input, memchr newline search, no UTF-8 validation, ahash, leaking large structures instead of freeing, multithreaded hashing and HyperLogLog for the estimate mode.
stars_or_usage: crates.io and AUR packages (per README); star count not seen
tradeoffs: Exact mode keeps every distinct line in memory; near-exact mode ignores 64-bit hash collisions; estimate mode is approximate; -c output is unsorted unless -s; hashing loses to sorting when nearly every line is unique.
caveats: First-party and Windows-only harness: the GNU baseline is coreutils 8.32 and gawk 5.3.2 under Git Bash, which may be a weaker baseline than a Linux build (sort thread count and flags unknown). The win is an algorithm change (hash versus sort), not a language effect. The author's own table also measures huniq 2.7.0 (6m04.595s count), runiq and sortuniq. GPL licence.

workload: Counting bytes, lines, words, characters and max line length of a 341,152,640-byte XML file (Dickens_Charles_Pickwick_Papers.xml) and of test-utf-8.html, single file and many files via xargs; timed with hyperfine-style 'times faster' output.

The -m rows compare a UTF-8-only counter with wc's locale-aware multibyte path, so they are not equal work, and the --threads row uses 12 threads against single-threaded wc. name: encodify (Rust Base64, Base32 and Quoted-Printable codecs)
baseline: simdutf (C++) Base64 codec, called through the simdutf Rust crate
workload: Criterion throughput (GB/s) of Base64 encode and decode, MIME Base64 with 76-column CRLF lines, Base32 and Quoted-Printable at 32 B, 1 KiB, 64 KiB and 1 MiB (cargo bench --bench codec).
claimed_speedup: README, 64 KiB, against the fastest other crate: Base64 encode 25.7 GB/s (1.0x simdutf) on Apple M5 Max NEON and 19.2 GB/s (1.0x base64-turbo) on AMD EPYC Zen 2; Base64 decode 18.1 GB/s (1.2x simdutf) and 15.0 GB/s (1.0x base64-turbo); MIME encode 21.3 GB/s (1.5x simdutf, LF only) and 10.7 GB/s (1.1x simdutf); MIME decode 14.1 GB/s (1.4x simdutf) and 8.6 GB/s (1.7x simdutf). Plain Base64 is parity with simdutf; at 32 B the Apple M5 MIME-encode row has simdutf (LF only) ahead, 5.75 GB/s vs encodify 4.50 GB/s, and base64-simd decodes 32 B faster than encodify (7.73 vs 6.08 GB/s).
compiler_and_flags: Criterion via 'cargo bench --bench codec'; rustc version and the C++ build flags of the simdutf crate are not stated (README shows RUSTFLAGS cfgs only for the AVX2-off and scalar variants).
hardware: Apple M5 Max (NEON) and AMD EPYC Zen 2 (AVX2)
why_faster: README: SIMD kernels for NEON and SSSE3/AVX2 with runtime detection, output appended to caller-owned buffers or slices without zero-filling or hidden reallocations.
tradeoffs: Mail-protocol oriented API (RFC 2045, 2047, 2152, 3501, 7468); SIMD only on NEON and x86 SSSE3/AVX2.
caveats: Brand-new first-party repo (published 2026-10-02) with 3 commits. The C++ baseline is the simdutf crate wrapper, and the simdutf rows are 'LF only' for MIME, so they do not emit the CRLF output encodify produces. Plain Base64 is parity, so the real wins over C++ are the MIME rows (1.1x to 1.7x). Outside the MIME case, base64-turbo and simdutf are within a few percent.

name: fast-float (Rust port of fast_float)
baseline: strtod from the C standard library (also compared: abseil C++, netlib C, fast_float C++)
workload: Parse one decimal string into a 64-bit float; best timing in ns per number on the canada, mesh, uniform, iidi, iei and rec32 datasets.
claimed_speedup: README tables, ns per number, fast-float vs strtod (C): Intel i7-4771 canada 21.58 vs 286.10, uniform 19.36 vs 258.73, mesh 10.70 vs 31.15; Apple M1 canada 14.84 vs 176.13, uniform 11.24 vs 165.43; AMD Rome canada 25.90 vs 123.37, uniform 20.54 vs 101.58, mesh 12.12 vs 65.68 (ratios of roughly 2.9x to 13x across all datasets, derived from page data). README text: 2-8x faster than Rust std FromStr, about 2-3x faster than the nearest competitors, and within noise of the original fast_float C++ library.
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.49; crate release profile sets lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1. Compiler and flags for the C and C++ rows are not stated (they come from lemire/simple_fastfloat_benchmark).
hardware: Intel i7-4771 3.5GHz (macOS), Apple M1 (macOS), AMD Rome (Linux)
why_faster: Direct port of Lemire's fast_float (Eisel-Lemire method): a fast path for inputs with at most 19 significant digits and a slower exact path for longer ones; the C strtod row uses a general arbitrary-precision approach (the second half is this agent's inference, the README names only the fast-path design).
tradeoffs: Parses decimal text to f32/f64 only (no formatting). No dependencies, no_std capable. Repo last committed July 2021 (crate 0.2.0 from January 2021).
caveats: The algorithm is Lemire's, already catalogued as fast_float (C++); the Rust port matches it within noise, so the win over strtod is algorithmic rather than a language advantage. Benchmarks are first-party, the Rust version is 1.49 and compiler flags for the C rows are missing, so the tier is C. The strtod row is whatever libc the machine had: macOS libc on the Intel and M1 rows, and (not stated, presumably glibc) on AMD Rome. Newer Rust standard-library releases may have narrowed the from_str gap (not checked this session). Included mainly as the Rust-side evidence for the algorithm.

name: fastgrep (Rust grep)
baseline: GNU grep 3.12 (C)
workload: Recursive searches over a generated corpus of 200 files x 5,000 lines of Rust-like source (sparse and dense matches, case-insensitive, regex, single 100k-line file) and a scaling test of 50 to 500 files.
claimed_speedup: README benchmark table (warm trigram index, LC_ALL=C): -rn 'fn main' 8.82 ms vs GNU grep 32.99 ms (3.74x); -rc 'use ' 8.55 ms vs 84.75 ms (9.91x); -rni error 37.49 ms vs 82.57 ms (2.20x); -rn 'impl\s+Drop' 45.24 vs 73.43 (1.62x); very sparse SubscriptionManager 5.41 vs 39.35 (7.28x); single file 3.70 vs 5.21 (1.41x); but -rl 'fn main' 7.50 ms vs GNU grep 7.12 ms (0.95x, GNU grep faster). Scaling: 1.48x at 50 files, 2.43x at 200, 3.08x at 500.
compiler_and_flags: fastgrep 0.1.9, Rust 1.99.0 release build, Criterion benchmarks; GNU grep 3.12 installed via Homebrew (build flags unknown).
hardware: Apple M2 Max (12 logical CPUs), 32 GB, macOS 27.0.1
why_faster: README: parallel by default across all CPU threads, lazy trigram index that skips non-matching files on repeat searches, SIMD-accelerated literal search.
tradeoffs: Output order is non-deterministic (multi-threaded); deliberate deviations from GNU grep (binary files, long lines). Index cache stored under the OS cache directory and invalidated by mtime and size. Not every GNU grep flag implemented.

Gains come mostly from 12-thread parallelism and a warm index versus single-threaded GNU grep, not from a faster per-byte scan; the README itself notes --no-index is often faster when the index cannot skip files. The same suite also builds 'Fast' (-O3 -march=native -mtune=native, thin LTO), 'Unsafe' (-O3 -march=native -ffast-math, full LTO) and 'PGO' (-O2 plus profile) variants; all non-instrumentation C and C++ rows were compared here. Rust: rustc 1.99.0 'cargo build --release'. Zig 0.17.0 'zig build build-zig'. Go 1.27.1 'go build'. (Versions and commands from the results file.)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37)
why_faster: Not stated by the suite. The loop is nearly identical in Go and C++; the Go key is a zero-copy substring plus strings.TrimSpace, while the C++ test copies the key with substr and trim (this agent's reading of the sources, small effect).

caveats: Tier capped at C: language-level claim with no mechanism given by the source (the zero-copy-key explanation is this agent's reading of the code). Small margin (18%) on a single run per configuration, so inside typical run-to-run noise for a 0.75 s test; kept only because the algorithm is the same in all languages. Go also loses badly on other text tests in the same suite (Etc::LogParser 30.9 s). LangArena calls itself 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. The headline C/C++ 'prod' rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3, LTO, PGO and fast-math variants were also compared and the non-C row still wins. The per-benchmark ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite. Rows were picked by this agent as text tests where a Rust, Zig or Go production row beats every C and C++ row; most other text tests in the suite go the other way (for example Base64::Encode and Base64::Decode, where C is about 3x faster than Rust, and Distance::Jaro, which is a tie).

name: hist-rs (hist, Rust unique-line counter)
baseline: sort | uniq -c | sort -n built from the system sort and uniq (coreutils; GNU or BSD not stated, the run was on macOS)
workload: Count unique lines of a random 1M-line FASTQ-style file generated with nucgen (-n 1000000 -l 20), piped through each tool, timed with hyperfine (warmup 10); second benchmark deduplicates the stream (hist -u).
claimed_speedup: README table (MacBook M3 Pro): hist 231.5 ms vs naive 'sort | uniq -c | sort -n' 5637.6 ms (24.4x, derived from page data; repo description says 25x), vs the same pipe with LC_ALL=C 1219.5 ms (5.3x derived) and with LC_ALL=C plus -S 1G 1179.2 ms (5.1x derived), vs awk count pipeline 1265.4 ms (5.5x derived), vs uutils coreutils pipeline 890.1 ms (3.8x derived). Dedup mode: hist 180.6 ms vs awk '!seen[$0]++' 1307.1 ms (7.2x derived).
compiler_and_flags: Cargo.toml release profile: lto = true, codegen-units = 1; .cargo/config.toml: -C target-cpu=native; edition 2024; rustc version not stated. Baseline tool versions and flags not stated; exact commands are in the repo's justfile.
hardware: MacBook M3 Pro (README)
why_faster: Not stated in the README. Inference from Cargo.toml (hashbrown, bumpalo): hash-table counting over an arena instead of an O(n log n) sort of all lines.
tradeoffs: Holds every distinct line in memory (a hash table), so memory grows with the number of unique lines; output order is by abundance rather than the stable sort order of uniq.
caveats: Most of the headline 24x comes from the default-locale sort: with LC_ALL=C the gap shrinks to about 5x. The input is random 20-character sequences, so almost every line is unique, which is not typical for duplicate-heavy data. First-party, one machine, no baseline versions; sort and uniq on macOS are probably the BSD versions. The speedup is algorithmic (hash counting vs sorting), not a language-level effect. Sibling tools huniq and cuniq are already recorded separately.

why_faster: README: a derivative-based, non-backtracking engine built for large alternations, lookarounds and boolean combinations (intersection, complement); on standard patterns it only matches the regex crate. The POPL paper (ACM DOI 10.1145/3704837, 'RE#') was not opened (host blocked).
stars_or_usage: 188 stars (Rust rewrite); the .NET version resharp-dotnet (258 stars) is already catalogued
tradeoffs: Leftmost-longest instead of leftmost-first match semantics; no capture groups or single-match find (is_match and find_all only); lazy quantifiers are parse errors; large alternations cost memory; capacity or lookahead overflow returns an error.
caveats: First-party table on a hand-picked set of 'popular crates.io patterns' (one row carries an unexplained asterisk); match semantics differ from PCRE2, so match counts are not guaranteed identical; PCRE2 version and compiler flags are not stated and PCRE2 comes through a Rust binding. The .NET sibling resharp-dotnet shows its large wins only over .NET regex, not over C engines. A peer-reviewed paper exists but was not readable here.
found_via: WebSearch 'RE# resharp regex engine .NET derivatives faster than RE2 Rust regex benchmark github ieviev'; README and resharp-engine/examples/popular-crates.rs read from raw.githubusercontent.com

name: runiq (Rust duplicate-line filter)
baseline: GNU sort -u and uniq (coreutils; versions not stated); also uq and huniq

name: sd (find and replace CLI)

GNU sed regex speed depends on locale (UTF-8 vs C), unstated. name: Spellbook (Rust Hunspell-format spellchecker, rewrite of Nuspell)
baseline: Hunspell and Nuspell (C++), single-word check()
workload: Criterion median time to check one word against the stock en_US dictionary for ten word shapes (in-dictionary, number, prefix and suffix stripping, title and upper case, hyphen breaks, compound), plus a Valgrind DHAT heap total for checking one word.
claimed_speedup: check(): 'earth' 42.82 ns vs Hunspell 197.25 ns and Nuspell 125.89 ns; '8675,309.0' 14.14 ns vs 220.89 and 112.92 ns; 'light-weight-like' 779.06 ns vs 4,329.10 and 1,248.90 ns; 'unearthed' 264.98 ns vs 405.81 and 521.53 ns. Not faster on every row: compound word '20000th' 676.08 ns vs Nuspell 656.35 ns (Hunspell 3,204.10 ns). DHAT total allocation for one check: Spellbook 2,580,386 bytes in 44,741 blocks vs Nuspell 4,437,599 bytes in 50,419 blocks and Hunspell 3,325,493 bytes in 90,736 blocks.
compiler_and_flags: Spellbook: cargo bench with Criterion (benches/check.rs). Hunspell and Nuspell: vendored C++ sources built through the cc crate in the-mikedavis/ffi-dictionaries and timed with nightly libtest #[bench]. No compiler versions, optimisation levels or flags are stated.
tradeoffs: Only check() is benchmarked; the author says dictionary load and suggestion matter less and does not measure them. Hunspell-format dictionaries. Rust crate; the repo ships no benchmark of its own against Hunspell, the C++ numbers come from a separate FFI harness.
caveats: First-party numbers, CPU and compiler not stated, so tier C. The two sides use different harnesses (Criterion vs nightly libtest, C++ called through FFI with c"word" literals). The word_with_suffix row is not apples to apples: the table lists 'earthed' but the ffi-dictionaries benches check 'earthly' (a literal stem in the dictionary, which skips suffix stripping) while Spellbook's check.rs now benches 'earthed' with a comment about that difference; the table row does not match the current benchmark sources. Spellbook is described as mainly a rewrite of Nuspell, so the win is implementation detail, not a new algorithm. The ffi-dictionaries harness is GPL-3.0. Only the en_US dictionary is in the table.
found_via: GitHub: helix-editor/spellbook README (Rust rewrite of Nuspell) links docs/compare.md; WebSearch 'Rust rewrite of C++ library faster than Nuspell OR hunspell...' returned the crate.
why_faster: Per the author: Spellbook uses hashbrown (SIMD group probing) with foldhash for the stem table where Nuspell rolls its own hash table with std::hash; Rust's standard library string search and equality are well optimised; small-string and small-slice optimisations cut memory. The author labels the string-search point a suspicion and does not profile it.

name: YARA-X (Rust rewrite of YARA)
baseline: YARA (VirusTotal/yara, the C implementation; the blog calls it 'YARA (legacy)', version not stated)
workload: Scanning files with YARA rules (multi-pattern Aho-Corasick string search plus regex and hex-pattern evaluation): full YARA Forge rule set over 500 random VirusTotal files (about 24 GB); single-rule docs examples (a Bitcoin-address regex over a ~200 MB file, and a for-loop rule).
claimed_speedup: Blog table (500 files, ~24 GB, YARA Forge rule set): YARA-X with daachorse 26.152 s, YARA (legacy) 48.275 s, which the blog states as 'YARA-X with daachorse is 1.85x faster'; the same table lists YARA-X with the previous aho_corasick crate at 57.584 s, i.e. slower than legacy YARA (about 1.19x slower, derived from page data). Docs page: the bitcoin_address regex rule on a ~200 MB file 'will take more than 20 seconds in YARA, but less than a second in YARA-X'; the 'for any i in (0..filesize-1)' rule 'will be 5-6x faster in YARA-X than in YARA'. Both pages say YARA-X is faster in almost all cases with a few exceptions where YARA is better.
why_faster: Blog (about the 2.2x gain over the previous YARA-X build, not directly versus YARA): swapping the aho_corasick crate for daachorse, a double-array Aho-Corasick with a tighter inner loop and cache-efficient storage; a later change groups many 'matches' regexes on one target into a single RegexSet pass. Docs give no mechanism for the regex and loop-rule gaps versus YARA beyond 'performs better ... with regular expressions and complex hex patterns'.
stars_or_usage: 1.3k stars; VirusTotal states it runs YARA-X in production
tradeoffs: Not a drop-in replacement: the C/C++, Python and Go APIs differ from YARA's (docs). No process scanning. A few rule semantics differ (docs 'differences with YARA'). Rust crate with C API in capi/.
caveats: First-party claim from the vendor (VirusTotal, Google) with no hardware, compiler flags, YARA version or build options, and the 500-file corpus is private, so the 1.85x figure is not reproducible by others; tier C. The same blog table shows YARA-X was slower than YARA (57.6 s vs 48.3 s) before the daachorse change, and the docs concede a few rules and files where YARA wins. The single-rule claims (20 s vs under 1 s; 5-6x) have no machine, file or version details and are about pathological rules that YARA itself warns on. The VirusTotal Livehunt figures in the blog (p99 over 6 s to under 3 s) compare YARA-X before and after a change, not YARA. I read the markdown sources of the blog and docs inside the repo (site/content/blog/yara-x-just-got-faster/index.md and site/content/docs/intro/yara_vs_yara-x.md), not the rendered virustotal.github.io pages (blocked here).

name: Zig (benchLANG strings workload, 19x19 word equality)
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0, `-O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops`, glibc memcmp per equal-length pair) and C++ (g++ same flags, std::string_view ==, libstdc++).
workload: benchLANG 'Strings': 5M iterations of comparing every pair of the 19 words of a constant sentence for equality (19x19 pairs per iteration).
claimed_speedup: README results table (Sept 2026, one run per language), Strings column: Zig 1.504 s, C 2.132 s, C++ 2.190 s, Go 2.532 s, Rust 2.621 s, Nim 2.804 s. Zig is 1.42x faster than C and 1.46x faster than C++ (derived from page data). Zig is not faster overall: on the Fibonacci workload Zig is 3.181 s vs C 1.694 s, and C ranks first on total runtime (9.762 s vs Zig 10.737 s).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0 `zig build-exe -OReleaseFast -mcpu=native -fstrip -lc`; C `gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s` and C++ `g++ -std=c++20` with the same flags, GCC 16.2.0 from nixpkgs-unstable.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz, 48 GB DDR4-3600, Arch Linux; one run per language, 3 September 2026
tradeoffs: ReleaseFast removes Zig's safety checks. The Nix flake pins every toolchain, and the analyzer marks the ranking invalid if checksums differ between languages (README).
caveats: The source states no mechanism, so this is capped at C. Reading the code (my inference, not the source's): both versions compare lengths first and then bytes; C calls memcmp for each equal-length pair while Zig's std.mem.eql is inlined, so the gap may be call overhead on tiny strings. The input is a 19-word compile-time constant (README warns constants can be folded), a single run per language, and Rust and Go are slower than C on the same task. The same repository ranks C first overall.

name: bitdp (compile-time derived bit-parallel alignment kernels)
baseline: edlib (C++), ksw2 extz2_sse (C) and parasail scan16/diag16 (C)
workload: Edit-distance and other linear-gap global alignment of independent DNA pairs (1 kbp and 150 bp sets, real Illumina reads, a 32-guide CRISPR scan of E. coli K-12), measured in GCUPS on one core with every tool's total cost cross-checked.
claimed_speedup: Batched bitdp is faster than edlib, ksw2 and parasail's correct kernels on every DNA workload measured: 35.2 GCUPS against 21.7 (edlib), 2.2 (ksw2) and 5.2 (parasail) for edit distance on 1 kbp pairs with AVX2; margin over edlib shrinks to 15% on real Illumina reads; CRISPR-style scan 0.30 s against 13.3 s for the plain DP. BLOSUM62 is several times slower than parasail.
compiler_and_flags: bitdp built with Zig 0.16.0 -Doptimize=ReleaseFast, once with -Dcpu=znver4 (AVX-512, 8 lanes) and once for AVX2; ksw2 commit 289609b built with gcc 15.2.0 -O3 -march=native; edlib and parasail are Ubuntu builds (flags not stated; the Ubuntu parasail has no AVX-512 kernels).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 8840U (Zen 4, AVX-512), Ubuntu under WSL2 (kernel 6.6.114.1), one core, no threading
tradeoffs: Research code, not yet stable; global and search modes with linear gap costs only; at most 32 distinct score differences and 24 substitution costs; compile-time derivation takes seconds to about 15 s (375 MB of compiler memory for BLOSUM62); batched mode needs many independent pairs to fill SIMD lanes.
caveats: Single author, single machine. The comparison is batched SIMD lanes (one alignment per lane) against single-pair tools, a different regime from edlib's per-pair banded algorithm; bitdp reaches only 0.73-1.20 of the closest hand-derived tool BGSA. Library baselines are distro builds. parasail's striped kernels were excluded because they returned wrong costs on some pairs. Headline figures are from the README Speed section; bench/RESULTS.md (also opened) holds the full tables (35.20 vs 21.73 edlib, 2.20 ksw2, 5.19 parasail scan16 on the 5,000-pair 1 kbp set).
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/bioinformatics?l=zig topic page
why_faster: Bit-parallel kernel derived at compile time from the recurrence (14 word operations per column for unit edit costs versus 15 for Myers) with one alignment per SIMD lane for independent pairs.

name: ckmeans (Rust optimal 1-D k-means) vs Ckmeans.1d.dp C++
baseline: Ckmeans.1d.dp C++ implementation (kmeans_1d_dp, methods 'linear' (default) and 'loglinear'; the code behind the R package and the ckmeans-1d-dp Python package), vendored in bench_cpp
workload: Optimal 1-D k-means (dynamic programming) on seeded random inputs: Uniform(1,3) and Uniform(0,1000) at n = 110,000 and 1,000,000, k from 3 to 50, a bimodal normal input, and BIC selection of k in 1..9; Criterion point estimates, one run of the full suite.
claimed_speedup: bench_cpp/README.md (Criterion, ms): Uniform(1,3) n=110,000 k=5 rust_indices 13.2 vs cpp_linear 26.0 and cpp_loglinear 25.3; k=20 49.7 vs 105.3 / 90.7; n=1,000,000 k=5 126.7 vs 254.9 / 249.8; k=20 513.5 vs 995.4 / 940.5; Uniform(0,1000) n=110,000 k=3 7.6 vs 16.5 / 16.1, k=50 114.4 vs 256.0 / 193.0; BIC selection n=110,000 rust_optimal 26.7 vs 54.5 / 50.9, n=1,000,000 263.1 vs 510.2 / 515.9. About 1.6x to 2.3x faster than C++ in every row, counting the slowest Rust variant (rust_optimal, which includes the BIC step) against the faster C++ method (derived from page data); the repository's PR #41 summary says 'Rust is 23 to 48 % faster than the C++ code in all cases'.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.99.0 with the bench_cpp release profile lto = true, codegen-units = 1 (same as the ckmeans_py release build); C++ sources compiled by build.rs with -O3 -DNDEBUG -std=c++11 using Apple clang 17.0.0 (no LTO, no -march stated).
hardware: Apple M2 Pro
tradeoffs: The vendored C++ code is LGPL-3.0-or-later and the Rust crate is BlueOak-1.0.0. Rust ckmeans_indices returns sorted data plus index ranges rather than per-value labels; the C++ call also returns labels, centres and sizes, and the Rust wrapper needs a mutex because kmeans_1d_dp() sorts through a static pointer. Results are identical to the scalar search (README).
caveats: Library win, not a language-level claim. Different implementations of the same objective: the Rust crate uses a flat matrix, a stack-based divide-and-conquer column fill with a single-pass inner loop and a vectorised split-point search (fearless_simd), while the C++ code is scalar; so the speedup mixes engineering, algorithm constant factors and SIMD. The C++ default call also does a BIC step (6 to 10 percent of its time) that rust_indices and rust_clusters skip; rust_optimal does it and is still faster. Single run of the suite on one aarch64 laptop, benchmark written by the crate author; the bench_cpp crate and its results were added in October 2026 commits (PR description links a Claude Code session). BlueOak-1.0.0 is a permissive licence that is not on the OSI-approved list, so usability is set to reference per the rubric; the orchestrator may override.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Rust crate README benchmark comparison with C++ library faster than abseil OR folly OR boost ...' surfaced urschrei/ckmeans PR #41; then opened bench_cpp/README.md, the crate README, Cargo.toml files and the commits page.
why_faster: Source (README, 'Implementation' table): flat contiguous matrix for cache locality, stack-based divide-and-conquer column fill with a single-pass inner loop that computes the sum of squares once per candidate (the two-pointer approach computes it twice), pre-allocated stack, and a vectorised split-point search with run-time SIMD selection.

name: zipir (Zig streaming DEFLATE-family compression library and CLI)
baseline: zlib-ng 2.3.3 (zlib and raw DEFLATE), ISA-L igzip, and bgzip with libdeflate 1.26 or zlib-ng (htslib 1.24)
workload: Single-threaded compression at levels 1/5/9 and decompression of gzip, zlib, raw DEFLATE and BGZF on FASTQ (57.2 MB and 20.2 MB), PRIDE XML, mzIdentML and Canterbury tar files, with output size reported beside speed.
claimed_speedup: zlib and raw DEFLATE decompression: zipir is the fastest tool, the fastest peer (zlib-ng) takes 1.24x its time (1.17-1.28x); zlib/raw DEFLATE compression: zlib-ng takes 1.35x zipir's time with 34% larger output at level 1, 1.08x with 2% larger at level 5 and 2.01x with 2% larger at level 9; gzip decompression level with ISA-L igzip (1.01x average, per-file 0.81-1.25); losses: bgzip+libdeflate is 1.07x faster on BGZF decompression and ISA-L igzip is faster at every gzip compression level (with 15-22% larger output).
compiler_and_flags: zipir 0.1.2 built with Zig 0.16.0 ReleaseFast -Dcpu=native, stripped, single-threaded; peers: zlib-ng 2.3.3 and libdeflate 1.26 as static libraries (bioconda configuration), htslib 1.24 default compiler flags with native-instruction codec libraries, ISA-L igzip.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (AVX2), Linux 7.2.7 (Fedora 44), one host, measured 2026-09-27
tradeoffs: Streaming library with fixed caller-owned memory (peak 0.55-0.62 MiB versus 1.6-5.0 MiB for the C tools); no dependencies; compression levels are zipir's own, so output sizes differ from zlib-ng at the same numeric level.
caveats: Report states it predates the current release: compression rows were measured at commit 5f25547 (marked with uncommitted changes) and decompression rows at ff8e9e8. Single host, first-party. Level numbers are not equivalent effort across tools, which is why output size is shown; the loses against ISA-L and libdeflate are documented in the same report. Very new repository.

name: zroar (Zig serialized Roaring bitmaps)
baseline: CRoaring 5.0.0 (roaring64 API, portable and frozen serialization)
workload: CRoaring's benchmark suite ported to Zig plus warm-open and cold-open variants and a zipfian OLTP synthetic dataset: contains, insert, remove, random access, set operations, cardinality, serialize and deserialize; 360 benchmark cases.
claimed_speedup: By design zroar performs 2x to 9x faster (geometric mean) than CRoaring on warm and cold opens and is faster in 339 of 360 cases; real data with bitmaps in memory 2.20x (36 tests), cold open 6.92x vs portable and 3.44x vs frozen (40 tests), synthetic operations 2.18x (132 tests), serialize plus deserialize 615x vs portable (56 tests), cardinality 4.8x geomean. CRoaring decisively wins (about 3x) on random interleaved insert/remove.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0, ReleaseFast; CRoaring 5.0.0 is compiled by the same zig build through addCSourceFiles with the croaringFlags helper in build.zig (AVX-512 toggled from target features), not by CRoaring's own CMake -O3 build.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5950X, performance governor, frequency fixed at 4.00 GHz, SMT on, benchmark process pinned to one core
tradeoffs: 64-bit integers only; no run container; does not read or write CRoaring's portable serialization format; random interleaved insert/remove is about 3x slower than CRoaring; pre-1.0 with calendar versioning and a format-version check.
caveats: Author benchmark of the author's own library. Much of the cold-open gain comes from the design (a serialized buffer usable without deserialization) rather than from Zig. Datasets built to showcase run containers were excluded because zroar has none. CRoaring is built through Zig's C toolchain, so its flags differ from an upstream CMake build. 27 commits in total, created August 2026. Headline figures are from the README; BENCHMARKS.md (also opened) holds the per-dataset ratio tables.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/compression?l=zig style Zig topic pages, then the zroar README and BENCHMARKS.md
why_faster: README 'Why Is It Faster': one contiguous buffer used in place with few dependent loads, versus CRoaring reaching a container through a chain of dependent loads and an adaptive radix tree index for the high 48 bits.

name: C3 compiler (c3c) compile throughput vs gcc and g++ in nordlow/compiler-benchmark
baseline: C (gcc 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang 23.1.1) and C++ (g++ 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang++ 23.1.1) compiling the same generated arithmetic translation unit
workload: nordlow/compiler-benchmark: compile (and run) one massive synthetic translation unit of arithmetic call chains, reported as microseconds per generated function ('Total=Build+Run [us/f]'), untemplated and templated variants.
claimed_speedup: README table, Total=Build+Run us/f (untemplated / templated): C3 153 / 255 vs C gcc-15 392, C gcc-16 454, C++ g++-15 303 / 600, C++ g++-16 486 / 566. About 2.6x faster than gcc-15 and 3.0x faster than gcc-16 on C untemplated (derived from page data); on the templated variant 255 vs g++-15 600 and g++-16 566 is about 2.2x to 2.4x faster (derived).
compiler_and_flags: Compiler versions are listed in the README table (zig 0.18.0-dev.35, odin dev-2026-09, c3c 0.8.5, rustc 1.100.0-nightly, gcc 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang 23.1.1); the README calls the test 'unoptimized code-generation scaling' and does not document optimization flags for any compiler.
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 (8+8 cores) at 5.09 GHz, Arch Linux, sample run as of 2026-09
license: MIT (compiler source under src is LGPL-3.0)
tradeoffs: Templated builds are 1.7x slower than untemplated (153 to 255 us/f); the compiler source is LGPL-3.0 while the rest of the repository is MIT.
caveats: Compile-time comparison on one synthetic file of arithmetic call chains with no headers, standard library or module resolution (the README says it does not reflect real builds), not the usual run-time -O3 comparison; C and C++ flags are undocumented so optimization levels are unmatched. C3 is slower than clang C (118 us/f) and clang++ templated (107 us/f), and the README conclusions say templated C3 code costs 77% more build time. The sibling record for D (dmd) is from the same table. Independent suite, but a small one (167 stars) and one machine.
found_via: GitHub: README of nordlow/compiler-benchmark (found by the sys shootouts search for D; this row and the other systems-language rows of the same table were not recorded there).
why_faster: README: no C3-specific mechanism is stated; the suite attributes the spread mostly to the cost of the GCC front end and optimizing backend.

name: D dmd compile throughput (nordlow/compiler-benchmark) vs clang, gcc, clang++ and g++
baseline: clang 23.1.1, gcc 15.3.0 and 16.2.1 (C) and clang++ 23.1.1, g++ 15.3.0 and 16.2.1 (C++) compiling the same generated arithmetic translation unit
workload: nordlow/compiler-benchmark: compile (and run) a single massive synthetic translation unit of arithmetic call chains, reported as microseconds per generated function for check, compile and Total=Build+Run, untemplated and templated variants.
claimed_speedup: D (dmd 2.113.0) Total=Build+Run 13 us/f untemplated (19 templated), compile 10.3 us/f, vs C (clang 23.1.1) 118 us/f, C++ (clang++ 23.1.1) 236 us/f (107 templated), C++ (g++-15) 303 us/f (600 templated), C (gcc-15) 392 us/f. About 9x faster than clang C and 23x faster than g++-15 untemplated (derived from page data). The README states 6x-38x. LLVM-based ldmd2 is 95 us/f and GCC-based gdc is 527 us/f, so the speed comes from dmd's own backend.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler versions listed in the README table (dmd 2.113.0-95551bb, ldmd2 1.43.0, gdc 16.2.1, clang 23.1.1, gcc 15.3.0, g++ 15.3.0, gcc 16.2.1); optimization flags are not stated in the README, which describes the test as 'unoptimized code-generation scaling'.
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 (8+8 cores) at 5.09 GHz, Arch Linux, sample run as of 2026-09
why_faster: README: dmd's custom backend and front end do little optimization work; comparing dmd with LLVM-based ldmd2 and GCC-based gdc on the same D source isolates backend cost (dmd about 6x faster than ldmd2 and about 38x faster than gdc).
tradeoffs: dmd generates less optimized code than LDC or GCC; this claim is about build time, not run time. In the README's table Zig (110 us/f) is on par with clang C (118) and Odin (147), C3 (153) and Rust (187) are slower than dmd but not faster than clang, so only dmd is a clear compile-time win.
caveats: Synthetic arithmetic call chains with no header parsing, standard-library or module resolution; the README says it does not reflect real builds. Baseline is not -O3: C and C++ flags are not documented, so the optimization levels are unmatched and the claim is a compile-time comparison, not the usual run-time one. The README prose and tables disagree slightly (11.5 vs 10.3 us/f). The repository's benchmark script (named 'benchmark') was not opened; the raw URL for 'benchmark.py' returned 404 and the plain 'benchmark' fetch returned a 6-byte body, so flags could not be read.

name: ixy network driver in Rust (C2Rust-transpiled unsafe build versus C)
baseline: ixy C user-space network driver packet forwarder (gcc, and clang with the same LLVM version)
workload: CPU cycles and instructions per forwarded 64-byte packet by the ixy forwarder at batch sizes 32 and 8 on an Intel 82599-class NIC, measured with CPU performance counters (paper: The Case for Writing Network Drivers in High-Level Programming Languages, ANCS 2019).
claimed_speedup: C2Rust-transpiled unsafe Rust forwards a packet in 91 cycles with 121 instructions against 94 cycles and 127 instructions for C at batch 32 (about 3% fewer cycles), also true when C is built with clang on the same LLVM version. The idiomatic safe Rust driver is slower: 100 vs 94 cycles (6%) at batch 32 and 120 vs 108 (11%) at batch 8.
hardware: Intel Xeon E3-1230 v3 per the Rust-vs-C document (the repo README names an E3-1230 v2 at 3.3 GHz for the throughput graphs)
tradeoffs: Faster variant is entirely unsafe transpiled Rust without bounds checks; the safe idiomatic driver pays about 65% more instructions that out-of-order execution mostly hides.
caveats: The 'Rust is faster than C (unless you want safety)' line is tongue-in-cheek and rests on a 3-cycle difference from one machine; compiler versions and flags are not stated in the pages I read, and the document says the C code 'didn't use the CPU to its full potential' without naming a mechanism. Hardware generation is inconsistent between the document and the README. Results are from the 2018-2019 paper era and the repo has been quiet since December 2022.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Rust rewrite outperforms original C implementation benchmark' surfaced ixy-languages/Rust-vs-C-performance.md
why_faster: Document reports fewer executed instructions per packet in the transpiled build (121 vs 127) but gives no deeper mechanism; for safe Rust it explains that out-of-order CPUs hide bounds-check overhead (IPC 2.09 vs 1.35).

name: mosdepth (Nim BAM/CRAM depth calculator)
baseline: samtools depth (C, htslib); README table also lists bedtools genomecov (C++) and sambamba depth (D)
workload: Per-base depth on a 30X whole-genome BAM/CRAM with one thread, 500-base window mean depth with three threads, and an exome BAM against 1,195,764 exons.
claimed_speedup: Per-base depth about 2x as fast as samtools depth (BAM: mosdepth 25:23 vs samtools 50:12, relative 1.98; CRAM samtools 1.79x slower); sambamba 5.71x and bedtools 5.31x slower; window depth genome-wide in under 9 minutes of user time with 3 threads (8:44, relative 0.34); exome in 1 minute 38 seconds on one CPU.
compiler_and_flags: Nim with --mm:refc required; build comment in nim.cfg: nim c -a -d:static -d:release mosdepth.nim with htslib built --with-libdeflate. Build flags of samtools and bedtools are not stated.
tradeoffs: Memory is about 32 bits times the longest chromosome (about 1 GB for chr1, against 27 MB for samtools); slower than samtools for small one-off regional queries; no gain past about 4 threads; links htslib (C) for decoding.
caveats: Tier B rests on the peer-reviewed paper cited by the README, which I did not open (publisher blocked); the table in the README lists no hardware or tool versions. Results date from 2017-2018 era samtools and htslib. mosdepth's default skips samtools-style mate-overlap correction unless enabled, and the accuracy check compared samtools depth defaults against mosdepth without overlap detection. The speedup is algorithmic, not a Nim-versus-C effect.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/bioinformatics?l=nim topic page (brentp/hts-nim ecosystem)
Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): Nim and D bioinformatics tools that beat C/C++ tools; github.com/brentp/mosdepth README opened on github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com
why_faster: README: depth is kept in an array that is incremented at each read start and decremented at its end, summed cumulatively at output; no extra allocations or objects, whereas samtools depth goes through the pileup machinery.

name: Rust regex crate in mariomka/regex-benchmark vs C PCRE2, C++ Boost.Regex and C++ std::regex

name: bzip2z (Zig bzip2 with SA-IS block sorting)
baseline: system bzip2 1.0.8 (C); pbzip2 1.1.13 reported as a third column
workload: Compression and decompression throughput of a 1.0 MB mixed-pattern buffer with the bundled bench-bzip2 tool, 3 iterations, single thread and 16 resolved threads.
claimed_speedup: Single thread: compress 18.64 vs 10.43 MB/s (1.79x), decompress 67.14 vs 69.38 MB/s (0.97x), output 265768 vs 265931 bytes; with threads=auto (16): compress 27.18 vs 10.33 MB/s (2.63x), decompress 68.65 vs 69.16 MB/s (0.99x).
compiler_and_flags: bzip2z: Zig 0.15.2, -Doptimize=ReleaseFast; system bzip2 1.0.8 and pbzip2 1.1.13 from a Nix dev shell (build flags not stated)
hardware: Apple M4 Max, Darwin 25.3.0 arm64, run 2026-01-15
tradeoffs: Library with C FFI plus a bzip2-compatible CLI; optional multi-stream (pbzip2-style) mode; clean-room rewrite so conformance is the main risk.
caveats: One 1 MB input pattern and three iterations; decompression is parity. The compression win comes from replacing bzip2's block sort with SA-IS, so outputs are not byte-identical to bzip2 and the gain is algorithmic. The threads=auto row adds parallel block compression that stock bzip2 lacks. First-party.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/compression?l=zig topic page
why_faster: README: SA-IS linear-time suffix array construction for the Burrows-Wheeler transform in place of bzip2's original block-sorting logic, plus optional concurrent block compression.

name: fast_rsync (Dropbox, Rust SIMD rsync algorithm)
baseline: librsync (C), through the librsync Rust bindings: whole::signature, whole::delta, whole::patch
workload: rsync signature calculation, delta computation (64 KB edit, random data, pathological collision case) and delta application on 4 MiB buffers (16 KiB for the pathological librsync run), criterion benchmarks in benches/rsync_bench.rs.
claimed_speedup: Signature of 4 MiB: fast_rsync 1.0696 ms (3.6519 GiB/s) vs librsync 5.8521 ms (683.51 MiB/s), README says 6X on AVX2 and 3-4X on SSE2-only CPUs. Delta, 64 KB edit: 7.0596 ms vs 7.4649 ms. Delta, random: 38.317 ms vs 42.758 ms. Pathological 16384-byte case: 6.2550 ms vs 50.185 ms (about 8x, derived from page data); the 4 MiB pathological run is too slow for librsync and is not listed. Apply: 284.20 us vs 400.30 us.
hardware: Intel Core i7-6820HQ @ 2.70 GHz (AVX2), described by the authors as a noisy laptop
tradeoffs: Only the legacy MD4 signature format is supported, not BLAKE2, and MD4 is insecure, so every applied delta must be verified with another hash. SIMD on x86, x86-64 and aarch64 with runtime detection. In-memory buffers only.
caveats: Only the signature step (SIMD rolling checksum and MD4) is a large win; the two realistic delta rows are 6% and 12% faster and the apply row 1.4x. The 8x pathological row reflects collision detection that librsync lacks (different behaviour, not only speed). Compiler flags, build profile of the librsync C library and librsync version are not stated in the README; benches/rsync_bench.rs was not opened, so the harness is unchecked (a verifier may lift the tier if the flags are visible there). Single noisy laptop. Not updated since 2024.
found_via: Blogs / talks: Rust ports of C libraries that beat the original; README benchmark section of dropbox/fast_rsync
why_faster: README: SIMD operations (AVX2 gives the 6X on signatures) for the rolling checksum and MD4; delta rows are bound by single-block MD4 and by hash-map lookups where Rust's built-in HashMap gives 'a slight advantage'; pathological inputs are detected instead of degrading.

claimed_speedup: Comma delimiter: hck -Ld, 1.198 s and hck -d, 1.649 s vs GNU cut 7.541 s and awk 4.993 s (README relative column: cut 6.30x and awk 4.17x the fastest hck run; about 4.6x and 3.0x vs plain hck -d, , derived from page data). Space delimiter after tr -s: hck 6.171 s vs cut 7.471 s.

caveats: README says the numbers are not authoritative. It is not stated whether the benchmarked hck was built with target-cpu=native or PGO. The README does not explain the -L flag used in the fastest rows. xsv, tsv-utils and choose are compared too; tsv-select (D) is within 1.4x of the fastest hck row.
