name: hexdump-rs (Rust hexdump -C replacement)
baseline: system hexdump -C (C; implementation and version not stated, likely util-linux or BSD hexdump)
workload: Canonical hex+ASCII dump (hexdump -C) of four files with hyperfine -m 100 --warmup 5: 10 MB from /dev/random, a 7.8 MB semi-random file (test.mca), an 8.5 MB file whose lines all differ (no squeezing) and a 1.1 GB file of zeros.
claimed_speedup: Hyperfine screenshots in the README (img/*.png): dev-random 708.6 ms vs 16.9 ms (42.00x faster); test.mca 617.1 ms vs 16.0 ms (38.62x); no-squeeze.bin 646.3 ms vs 17.1 ms (37.86x); zeros.bin 658.2 ms vs 338.5 ms (1.94x). README text says 'up to a 14x speedup' while the repository description says 'up to 40x faster'.
compiler_and_flags: cargo release build (./target/release/hexdump-rs); Cargo.toml release profile only adds debug = true for flamegraphs; no C build flags (system hexdump binary as installed).
tradeoffs: Implements only hexdump -C, not hexdump's format-string language, and is 'meant as a drop-in replacement for hexdump -C' only.
caveats: Different algorithm: the system hexdump drives a generic format-string interpreter while this tool hard-codes the one canonical layout, so the 40x gap is a specialisation effect, not a language effect (my inference; the README gives no mechanism). CPU, OS, hexdump version and output destination are not stated, the numbers exist only as images, and the README text (14x) disagrees with the screenshots (up to 42x). The zeros.bin row (1.94x) is where both tools squeeze repeated lines. Tiny hobby repo with no stars.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Rust rewrite of C tool faster than original C benchmark hyperfine github faster than GNU' surfaced the hexdump-rs README; opened the README, the four screenshots and the commits page.

name: Koka (Perceus reference counting): cfold benchmark vs C++ gcc 9.3.0
baseline: C++ (gcc 9.3.0) version of the constant-folding benchmark in test/bench/cpp; it never reclaims memory, per the README
workload: cfold: constant folding over a large symbolic expression, an allocation-heavy benchmark with little computation.
claimed_speedup: README chart (values printed on the bars, relative to Koka = 1.00): execution time C++ 3.33 (Koka 3.33x faster); peak working set C++ 2.94x of Koka. Same chart, other rows: deriv C++ 1.33x slower; rbtree C++ 0.92 and nqueens C++ 0.79 (C++ faster than Koka there).
compiler_and_flags: Koka 2.0.3 compiled to C and built with gcc 9.3.0 (flags not stated in the README; test/bench builds through CMake, default build type Release); C++ built with gcc 9.3.0.
hardware: 3.8 GHz AMD 3600XT, Ubuntu 20.04, November 2020; averages over 10 runs
tradeoffs: Reference counting with in-place reuse needs no tracing GC but adds refcount work and cannot reclaim cycles; Koka compiles through C so any C toolchain can build it; much smaller ecosystem than C++.
caveats: Numbers are read from a chart image in the README (Koka 2.0.3, gcc 9.3.0, November 2020) and flags are not in the README. The C++ version allocates every node with new and never frees (README), so the baseline is allocator-bound and not an idiomatic or tuned C++ solution; a pooled or arena C++ version was not tried. Mixed results across the five benchmarks (C++ wins rbtree and nqueens). The Perceus paper was not opened (blocked).
found_via: GitHub: README of koka-lang/koka (benchmark section and chart doc/bench-amd3600-nov-2020.png), listed as a lead without numbers by the sys papers search; I read the values printed on the chart bars.
why_faster: Source (README): precise Perceus reference counting with reuse analysis, compiled to C 'without needing a garbage collector or runtime system'; the README frames the benchmarks as showing reference counting is viable and competitive, not as a direct absolute-speed comparison across languages.

The report appendix also covers Gemma 4 26B-A4B and H100 SXM.

name: mk1 (c-blake/bu, Nim up-to-date check for 1-to-1 build rules)
baseline: ninja (C++) and GNU make (C); the table also times a bash while-read loop
workload: Up-to-dateness check of 40,000 input/output file pairs in /dev/shm (nothing to rebuild), timed with the author's ru tool; mk1 reads a precomputed list of path pairs and prints the commands to run.
claimed_speedup: mk1 0.039390 s wall vs ninja with .ninja_log present ('no work to do') 0.119358 s (about 3.0x, README says ~3X faster than ninja's best case), ninja without a log 7.777944 s, ninja with the author's restat hack 0.410272 s, GNU make 1.550844 s (README: about 40X worse than mk1), bash loop 0.151993 s (about 4X).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for mk1 (Nim build flags); the page says the machine runs 'Linux 6.2.10 built w/gcc-12', wording unclear whether this refers to the kernel or the binaries; ninja and make versions not stated
hardware: Intel i7-1270P (Alder Lake), Linux 6.2.10, RAM file system (/dev/shm)
tradeoffs: Only handles the case where each output comes from exactly one input by one rule; no dependency graph, no depfile handling, no rule language, and it emits commands for a shell to run rather than running them.
caveats: Compares a deliberately restricted tool with general build systems on a special case; ninja's cost is dominated by its log handling and the author's own hacks. Different problem from ninja's, so same_algorithm is false. Build flags for mk1 and tool versions are missing; the shell script on the page is complete and short, so a verifier could rerun it. First-party measurement by the author, single machine.
found_via: Blogs / talks: c-blake/bu doc pages with README-level timings against C tools
why_faster: Page: only a freshness check for many 1-to-1 pairs is done (about 60 lines of Nim originally, about 150 now, per the page's footnote), with no graph or log; the author attributes make's cost to subshell delegation and ninja's best case to its .ninja_log reuse.

name: Nim 2.2.10 (ref objects): benchLANG binary trees vs C and C++ at -O3
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off) and C++ (g++ -std=c++20, same flags); both malloc/new every node and free (delete) it inside the timed region
workload: CLBG-style binary trees, depths 4 to 18: allocate, check and drop complete binary trees of individually allocated nodes; benchLANG's fifth workload (the others are primes, Fibonacci(45), strings and Mandelbrot).
claimed_speedup: README results table (September 2026, one run per language): Nim 0.809 s vs C 1.010 s and C++ 1.147 s on binary trees, about 1.25x faster than C and 1.42x faster than C++ (derived from page data). Other columns, Nim vs C: primes 2.725 vs 2.725 s, Fibonacci 1.716 vs 1.694 s, strings 2.804 vs 2.132 s, Mandelbrot 2.244 vs 2.201 s; total 10.298 s vs 9.762 s, so C is faster overall.
compiler_and_flags: Nim 2.2.10: nim c --nimcache:nimcache -d:danger -d:lto --panics:on --passC:-march=native --passC:-ffp-contract=off --passL:-s (C backend compiler not stated, nixpkgs GCC 16.2.0 presumably); C: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s; C++: g++ -std=c++20 with the same flags. Toolchains pinned with Nix.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz, 48 GB DDR4-3600 CL16, Arch Linux; one run per language, 3 September 2026
tradeoffs: Peak RSS for the whole process is 51.5 MiB for Nim vs 33.3 MiB for C; Nim loses to C on the strings workload (2.804 s vs 2.132 s).
caveats: The source gives no mechanism, which caps this at tier C. Reading languages/Nim/bench.nim and languages/C/bench.c (my inference): Nim uses 'ref object' nodes with no explicit free, so the runtime's own allocator and deterministic reference counting do the allocation and freeing, while C pays glibc malloc and free per node; a pooled or arena C version would likely erase the gap. One run per language, one machine, tiny suite, the README says its inputs are compile-time constants. Other languages beat C on this workload too (Java 0.347 s, OCaml 0.865 s, C# 0.931 s, Bun 0.816 s, Fortran 0.986 s), which points at allocator behaviour rather than Nim.
found_via: GitHub: raw README of GlebOlsen/benchLANG (the repo surfaced in the WebSearch 'faster than the C implementation benchmark Rust OR Zig OR Nim OR D'); I read every language column and the Nim and C sources. Sibling searches recorded Java, OCaml, C# and Zig rows from the same table; Nim was not recorded.

name: procs (c-blake, Nim ps, pgrep and pkill replacement: pd, pf, pk)
baseline: procps ps ('/bin/ps ax'), pgrep and pkill (C)
workload: Listing all processes with a minimal format (pid and command) to /dev/null, and finding a process by name over roughly 200 to 320 processes (pf -e1 vs pgrep -x), measured with the author's tim/tails tools under chrt 99 taskset.
claimed_speedup: README footnote: pd -f%p %c 2.8576 ms +- 0.0070 vs /bin/ps ax 5.0281 ms +- 0.0063 (README says roughly 2X; about 1.76x derived from page data); with process typology and highlights on, 3.9739 ms +- 0.0044, 1.27X faster than stock ps; pgrep and pkill are 5.025 +- 0.015X and 5.745 +- 0.016X slower than pf and pk on a 4-core and a 20-core CPU. bench.sh comments: pf -e1 init 1014.1 us vs pgrep -x init 7724 us (i7-6700K, 'up to 7.617 times faster') and 582.7 us vs 5539.6 us (i7-1370P, 9.507 times).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark; README build line is 'nim c -d:release --path:../cligen procs' (C backend compiler version not stated); procps version not stated
hardware: i7-6700K (no HT, 4.7 GHz) and i7-1370P in bench.sh; the machine for the README ps timings is not named
tradeoffs: Linux /proc only. Fewer canned formats than ps (it is a construction toolkit with config files); pd/pf/pk are symlinks to one binary. Author calls it 'a work in progress'.
caveats: The gains come from doing less work (reading only /proc/PID/stat when the format needs nothing else, where procps opens and parses both stat and status), so it is a different, narrower program rather than the same algorithm. Author says there are configurations where ps can be faster. The README timing machine and flags are unstated; bench.sh needs the author's tim and tails tools. Millisecond-scale wins on a single-user tool.
found_via: Blogs / talks: Nim/D/Zig tools with README timings against C utilities (c-blake GitHub projects), after the Nim topic pages gave nothing
why_faster: README: 'tries hard not to make unnecessary system calls', for example only opening /proc/PID/stat for a pid-and-command format while procps ps also opens and parses /proc/PID/status (the author says this makes pd roughly 2X faster).

name: regex (Rust regex crate) as measured in the rebar barometer
baseline: PCRE2 (interpreter and JIT), RE2 and Hyperscan
metric: throughput (search time); compile time is also reported
workload: rebar curated benchmark groups (literal, literal-alternate, date, ruff-noqa, lexer-veryl, cloud-flare-redos, unicode-character-data, words, aws-keys, bounded-repeat, unstructured-to-json, dictionary, noseyparker, quadratic) over haystacks such as OpenSubtitles text.
claimed_speedup: Search-time geometric mean of speed ratios to the best engine per benchmark (lower is better; 2025-12-19 record): hyperscan 2.37 (28 benchmarks), rust/regex 3.08 (38), pcre2/jit 6.00 (34), re2 10.39 (31), pcre2 interpreter 114.75 (33). Engines ran different benchmark subsets, so these means are not a common-subset comparison. Single rows: sherlock-en 29.4 GB/s rust/regex vs 26.3 pcre2/jit, 12.1 re2, 32.0 hyperscan; sherlock-ru 35.6 GB/s vs 32.8, 768.1 MB/s, 4.3 GB/s; but sherlock-casei-en 10.5 GB/s vs 18.8 pcre2/jit and 29.2 hyperscan.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README. Rust engines are release builds by rebar's harness; PCRE2, RE2 and Hyperscan are built by rebar's engine scripts with flags not shown on the pages opened.
hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i9-12900K (from record/curated/2025-12-19/lscpu.txt in the rebar repo)
tradeoffs: Linear-time guarantees (no backreferences or lookaround), so it is not a drop-in for PCRE2 features. Compile time is much worse than PCRE2 in rebar (compile-time geometric mean 11.85 vs 1.41 for plain PCRE2 and 6.20 for PCRE2 JIT).
caveats: The suite is written and run by the regex crate's author, and the README calls its results a 'curated and biased' set whose analysis is mostly about the Rust crate. Hyperscan has a better search-time mean (2.37) and wins several rows, and PCRE2 JIT wins the case-insensitive literal rows. The record is close to tier A (public harness, lscpu.txt recorded) but build flags of the C engines were not confirmed, so it is left at C for the verifier to retier. Means cover different benchmark counts per engine.
found_via: Looked up the rebar README results after the memchr README pointed at it; rust-lang/regex page says benchmarks moved to rebar
why_faster: The rebar README attributes wins to literal optimizations and prefilters: memchr and the Teddy SIMD multi-substring algorithm (ported out of Hyperscan), lazy DFA, one-pass DFA and a Pike VM fallback selected by a meta engine.

name: Rewrite it in Rust: A Computational Physics Case Study (Veytsman, Zhai, Ding, Sefkow)
baseline: The authors' C++ implementation of the same physics simulation (compiler and flags not seen)
workload: A computational physics simulation implemented in C++ and in Rust (plus a parallel Rust version), compared across test cases.
claimed_speedup: Per the arXiv abstract as returned by a search snippet (paper not opened): Rust runs faster than C++ in some test cases, 'as much as a 5.6x performance increase'.
tradeoffs: Unknown; the study also reports a parallel Rust version.
caveats: Snippet only: arxiv.org is blocked here and no code repository was found. Algorithm equivalence, compiler flags and the mechanism are unknown, so same_algorithm and same_opt_level are null; no mechanism means tier C at most. Contrast: the ASE 2022 study 'Towards Understanding the Runtime Performance of Rust' (Zhang et al.) reports Rust 1.77x slower than C on average for same-algorithm micro-benchmarks, and 'Is Rust C++-fast?' (arXiv 2209.09127) reports Rust similar to C++ with a minor disadvantage.

workload: u32, u64 and string keys, sizes 100 to 1M elements, 16 operation mixes (random and sequential insert, reserved insert, update, lookup hit and miss, tombstone, delete, iteration, churn, mixed, read-heavy, write-heavy, zipfian); ns per operation; C++ tables called through FFI.

BENCHMARKS.md, 100-element u32 set: Reserved Ins. 5 ns vs Abseil 13 / Boost 14 / Ankerl 9; Delete 4 ns vs 13 / 6 / 6; Lookup Miss 1 ns vs 5 / 2 / 3; Tombstone 5 ns vs 16 / 6 / 8. Losses in the same table: Rand. Lookup 3 ns vs Boost 2 ns, Write-Heavy 12 ns vs Ankerl 8 ns.
compiler_and_flags: Zig ReleaseFast; C++ compiler and flags not stated

Boost wins several lookup rows and Ankerl wins write-heavy rows in the table I read, so 'on average faster' rests on the README's aggregate plots (PNG, not readable). FFI to C++ adds overhead to the baseline. Verstable (C) is the algorithmic inspiration, not a benchmark target; the string fast path (strings up to 8 bytes packed in a u64) is not used by the competitors.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/performance?l=zig description 'faster than the top C++ hash tables'; README and BENCHMARKS.md of ThobiasKnudsen/verztable.

claimed_speedup: 42 ms vs 87 ms with IPADIC (about 2.1x, derived from page data) and 75 ms vs 179 ms with UniDic (about 2.4x, derived from page data). The raw-connector UniDic model takes 1364 ms and the dual-connector model 170 ms, about MeCab's UniDic time.

hardware: Intel Core i9-12900K (16 cores), 64 GB DDR5, Ubuntu 22.04
tradeoffs: Reimplementation of MeCab's minimum-cost method; models must be compiled into Vibrato's format. The UniDic model is 717 MB in the standard form, and the smaller variants trade speed (252 MB raw-connector at 1364 ms, 300 MB dual-connector at 170 ms).
caveats: First-party benchmark (README figure plus wiki), MeCab build flags unknown, single corpus and machine. The two NLP2023 conference papers listed in the README are about cache efficiency and CRF score splitting; their numbers were not opened.
found_via: Checked READMEs of Rust library crates with C/C++ originals; README points to the Speed-Comparison wiki
why_faster: README: cache-efficient id mappings for the large connection matrix, plus a simplified implementation of the MeCab algorithm.

name: Zig (kostya/benchmarks base64)
baseline: Hand-written scalar C base64 (no library), gcc and clang, -O3 -march=native -flto
workload: Base64 encode and decode of a 131072-byte string, 8192 tries, into newly allocated buffers; seconds.
claimed_speedup: Zig 0.703 s vs C/clang 0.918 s and C/gcc 1.117 s (about 1.3x and 1.6x faster, derived from page data). Rust 0.842 s is also faster than both. The same table has C/clang with aklomp/base64 at 0.095 s and C/gcc (aklomp) 0.097 s, about 7x faster than Zig.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0: zig build-exe -O ReleaseFast -lc (std.base64); C and C++: gcc/g++ 16.1.0 or clang/clang++ 22.1.8 with -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -std=c23 / c++23 -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries (common/commands.mk)
caveats: No mechanism is given by the source, which caps the tier at C. Zig uses its standard-library base64 while C is a separate hand-written table-driven implementation, so this compares two implementations, and the best C implementation (aklomp SIMD library) is far faster than Zig. The README states no compiler flags in prose; flags were read from common/commands.mk and the base64 Makefile. Values are medians with MAD from one machine.
found_via: GitHub: kostya/benchmarks README tables (cross-language suite named in QUEUE.md section E).
tradeoffs: Single task microbenchmark; Zig std.base64 is scalar.

name: ziggit (Zig git reimplementation)
baseline: git (C) CLI: status, log -20, branch -a, blame
workload: hyperfine (100 runs, 5 warmups) of small git commands in a test repository on macOS arm64, plus in-process library calls versus spawning git as a subprocess for a bun-style workflow.
claimed_speedup: README: 4-10x faster than git on macOS arm64: status 8.1 ms vs 1.0 ms (8.1x), log -20 8.4 vs 1.7 ms (5.0x), branch -a 7.9 vs 1.4 ms (5.6x), blame on a large repo 36 vs 2.8 ms (12.6x); as a library: findCommit 85x (macOS arm64) and 6x (Linux x86_64), cloneBare 7x and 34x, full workflow 10x and 32x.

hardware: macOS arm64 (CPU model not stated); Linux x86_64 for some library rows
tradeoffs: Drop-in git CLI plus Zig library, WASM build (142 KB), built-in git server and a succinct output mode for LLM use; GPL-2.0; feature parity with git tracked through git's own test suite results.
caveats: Sub-10 ms commands on small repositories are dominated by process start and file-system latency, so the multipliers say little about throughput on large repositories; the library rows measure in-process calls against spawning a subprocess, an overhead difference not an algorithm difference; git version unspecified; first-party.
found_via: WebSearch: 'pure Zig implementation benchmark faster than C reference library' (github.com results)

name: ZLB (Zig Language Benchmark) Mandelbrot SIMD row
baseline: C Mandelbrot with 4-lane SIMD intrinsics, gcc 16.1.1 and clang 22.1.8 at -O3 -march=native -ffp-contract=off (also zig cc)
workload: Mandelbrot set calculation, hyperfine mean of 20 runs after 1 warmup, wall-time ratio against the scalar gcc build (1.00x).
claimed_speedup: Time ratio vs scalar gcc: zig_simd_fast 0.16x and zig_simd_safe 0.18x against c_simd_clang 0.26x, c_simd_gcc 0.27x, rust_simd 0.27x, c_simd_zigcc 0.27x (Zig SIMD about 1.6-1.7x faster than the C SIMD builds); scalar rows are parity (zig_std_fast 1.00x, c_std_gcc 1.00x, c_std_clang 1.02x). Other rows in the same suite: sieve zig_static_bitset_fast 0.63x vs c_std_gcc 1.00x, btree zig_compact_fast 0.19x vs c_arena_gcc 0.21x, log_proc zig_std_fast 0.83x vs c_std_gcc 1.00x.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0 zig build-exe -O ReleaseFast (native CPU, README says -mcpu=native); C: gcc 16.1.1 and clang 22.1.8 with -O3, SIMD C rows add -march=native -ffp-contract=off, scalar C rows use -O3 only (Makefile read); Rust 1.97.1 opt-level=3 with LTO
hardware: Linux 7.1.4-arch; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Informal suite of five small benchmarks (mandel, sieve, btree, log_proc, atomics) in Zig, C, Rust, Go, Python and Bash.
caveats: Not like-for-like: the Zig SIMD kernel uses 8-lane f64 vectors while the C and Rust SIMD kernels use 4-lane intrinsics, scalar C rows lack -march=native while Zig builds natively, and the sieve and btree wins come from different data layouts (bitset, 32-bit indices), not the language. Single commit, single unnamed machine.
found_via: WebSearch: 'written in Zig faster than C library benchmark' (zff.dev mirror of tsukumoakito/zlb), then github.com/topics/benchmark?l=zig
why_faster: Source: Zig's @Vector with 8-lane f64 fills the CPU's execution units better than the 4-lane intrinsics used in C and Rust, and gives LLVM clearer intent.

name: zog (Zig SIMD JSONL search engine)
baseline: jq (C); the README column is labelled jq/jaq and also lists ripgrep
workload: Queries over a 1 GB JSONL dataset (6.7 million lines): key match, substring match, numeric comparison, TSV field extraction, JSON reformatting, aggregation and OR/AND logic, in GB/s.
claimed_speedup: zog (file) 4.03 GB/s simple key match vs 0.07 GB/s for jq/jaq, 2.83 GB/s field extraction vs 0.10, 2.41 GB/s aggregation vs 0.05; 20-50x faster than jq/jaq for typical queries; also faster than ripgrep (2.30 GB/s) and 4.1x faster on complex logic (2.24 vs 0.54 GB/s).
compiler_and_flags: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast; jq, jaq and ripgrep versions and flags not stated
hardware: 'modern NVMe SSD' only; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Does not fully parse JSON: byte-level SIMD key scanning in 8 MB blocks with a background reader thread, so malformed JSON and escaped keys may behave differently from jq; narrower query language.
caveats: First-party numbers with no versions, flags or CPU. jq and jaq (Rust) share one column so the C baseline alone is not separable. zog does a different, lighter job than jq (no AST, no validation), so the multiplier compares different semantics.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/simd?l=zig topic page
why_faster: README: skips building an AST (jq bottlenecks near 0.04 GB/s on it) and scans 32-byte chunks with AVX2/NEON bitmasks while a producer thread reads the next 8 MB block.

name: C# NativeAOT minima-sync (HttpArena entry)

name: cblt
baseline: nginx (Docker image nginx:latest per benchmark/nginx/Dockerfile)
workload: Apache Benchmark, 3000 requests at 1000 concurrent connections, downloading a 23 KB logo.png from 127.0.0.1; response-time percentiles.
claimed_speedup: Percentile table (units not stated, ab reports ms): 50%: 179 vs nginx 1209 (6.75x lower, derived from page data); 75%: 194 vs 1655 (8.53x); 100%: 200 vs 2146 (10.73x). README feature list: '10 times faster than Nginx for small content under 100KB'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (Cargo.toml: tokio, httparse, rustls, async-compression); nginx from the nginx:latest image
tradeoffs: Minimal file server and reverse proxy with load balancing, Docker label integration and TLS; far fewer features than nginx.
caveats: Single run of one 23 KB file; hardware, OS, ab flags beyond -c/-n, nginx config and the unit of the table are not stated; the '10x faster for content under 100KB' headline is supported by one file only. The repo has benchmark/ab.md (ab -c 100 -n 300 on logo_huge.png) with no numbers. A percentile table at 1000 connections for 3000 requests mostly reflects connection queueing, not steady-state throughput. Last commit June 2025.
found_via: WebSearch 'Rust web server benchmark faster than nginx wrk requests per second static files' and crates.io API search q='faster than nginx' (cblt: 'Safe and fast minimalistic web server, written in Rust')

name: D (LDC, betterC) port of the C epoll raw HTTP responder (httpbench)
baseline: the C epoll raw HTTP responder in the same suite (c/epoll/http_epoll.c, gcc -O3), same fixed 'Hello, World!' reply, prefork over 2 CPUs
workload: Fixed-response HTTP/1.1 keep-alive responder (no parsing, no routing) under wrk for 30 s at 2, 8, 64, 128 and 256 connections, plus 256 connections with pipeline depth 10; level-triggered and edge-triggered variants, prefork over 2 pinned CPUs.
claimed_speedup: No claim in the README; the tables show parity. Level-triggered D vs C RPS: 43752 vs 39886 (2 clients), 93942 vs 88906 (8), 176532 vs 187141 (64), 232039 vs 226433 (128), 276433 vs 261440 (256), 2075254 vs 2132917 (pipelined); edge-triggered D vs C: 43096 vs 39911, 86692 vs 85850, 166672 vs 173116, 234975 vs 216984, 261737 vs 258486, 1938169 vs 2005563. Ratios 0.94x to 1.10x (derived from page data); D ahead in 8 of 10 non-pipelined cells (behind at 64 clients) and about 3% behind in both pipelined cells.
compiler_and_flags: D: ldc2 1.29.0, --betterC plus default --release -O3 --boundscheck=off --ffast-math --mcpu=native (_suite/runner.d); C: gcc -Wall -O3 -D_GNU_SOURCE (c/epoll/Makefile), gcc version not stated (Docker image debian:testing build-essential).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X (8 cores, 16 threads) host, Fedora 36, kernel 5.17.9; server in a KVM VM with 2 pinned CPUs and load generator (wrk 4.1.0) in a KVM VM with 14 pinned CPUs, both Ubuntu 22.04 (bridged network)
tradeoffs: betterC @nogc D, i.e. D used as a C replacement without druntime, GC or exceptions; a micro benchmark that does not parse HTTP, so it says nothing about a real server.
caveats: This is a parity data point, not a win: counting the 10 non-pipelined cells, D is ahead in 8 and behind in 2 (64 clients, both variants) by at most 10%, and behind by about 3% (0.97x level, 0.97x edge) when pipelined; single 30 s runs with no variance reported, so the differences are probably noise. The D build uses --mcpu=native and --ffast-math while the C build uses plain -O3 without -march=native, so SIMD target is not matched (irrelevant for a syscall-bound loop). The C code is frevib's echo server slightly modified and the D file is a near line-by-line port using libc calls. The source states no mechanism and no claim (the suite's own C directory README says the D variants exist to test performance issues of the during library), which caps the tier at C. Unlicense is a public-domain dedication with no patent grant. Last commit 2022-05-30.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'same HTTP server implemented in C++ Rust Go Zig io_uring epoll comparison benchmark github repo' surfaced tchaloupka/httpbench.

name: during (D io_uring wrapper)
baseline: C liburing echo server (MarkReedZ/mrloop) and C++ epoll echo server (methane/echoserver), both built with -O3; in the httpbench suite also the C liburing HTTP-reply server
workload: Single-threaded echo server, 50 clients, 512-byte messages, 10 s, best of 3, driven by haraldh/rust_echo_bench on loopback; second data set is a fixed-reply HTTP responder under wrk at 2 to 256 connections in tchaloupka/httpbench.
claimed_speedup: echo_server README: during 131090 req/s vs C liburing server 95894 req/s vs C++ epoll server 45063 req/s (1.37x and 2.91x, derived from page data). httpbench README (separate harness, D port of the C liburing server, RPS from the tables): during/raw vs C io_uring raw is 41404 vs 37872 (2 clients), 86500 vs 75711 (8), 150752 vs 155627 (64), 221916 vs 185000 (128), 253256 vs 246812 (256), 2012380 vs 1898736 (256 clients, pipeline depth 10), i.e. 0.97x to 1.20x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: during echo server: dub build -b release --compiler=ldc2, ldc2-1.18.0. Baselines: built with -O3 and no -g (compiler name and version not stated). httpbench D builds: ldc2 1.29.0 with --betterC --release -O3 --boundscheck=off --ffast-math --mcpu=native; C baseline gcc -Wall -O3 -D_GNU_SOURCE -luring (gcc version not stated, liburing cloned from axboe/liburing at build time).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X 8-Core, Fedora 31 Linux 5.3.12 (echo_server README); httpbench: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X (8 cores, 16 threads) host, Fedora 36, kernel 5.17.9; server in a KVM VM with 2 pinned CPUs and load generator (wrk 4.1.0) in a KVM VM with 14 pinned CPUs, both Ubuntu 22.04 (bridged network)
tradeoffs: D library (druntime or betterC), Linux 5.7+ io_uring only; the echo example preallocates fixed io buffers registered with io_uring and can exceed the memlock limit; the library does not use liburing, so it reimplements the ring handling in D.
caveats: First-party numbers from the library author. The baselines are different programs, not a port: mrloop is an event-loop library and the C++ epoll echo server is a generic echo server, whereas the during example uses a fixed memory pool and buffer swapping, so the echo comparison is not same-algorithm. The echo README numbers come from 2019-era tools (ldc2-1.18.0, Linux 5.3.12, io_uring just introduced) and best-of-3 on loopback with one client machine; compiler versions of the baselines are missing. The httpbench rows are single 30 s runs per cell on a 2-vCPU server VM; the D port beats the C port in 5 of 6 cells (up to 1.20x) and loses by 3% at 64 clients, which is within plausible run-to-run noise for single runs, and the D build adds --mcpu=native while the C build does not. The httpbench README itself says the D variants exist to test performance issues of the during library, not to claim a win. The during README makes no performance claim and only points to the echo example. The echo-server category fits 'serving' loosely: it is a socket event loop, not an HTTP server.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch for a same-HTTP-server-in-several-languages comparison led to github.com/tchaloupka/httpbench, whose C-versus-D raw servers pointed to the during library and its echo_server README.
why_faster: io_uring with provided buffers and fixed pre-registered io buffers (README design notes); the source does not explain why it beats the C liburing server.

name: fib
baseline: Sogou workflow (C++ HTTP server) and uSockets (C, BoringSSL) in the lesismal go-*-benchmark repositories; nginx (C) in HttpArena
workload: HTTP/1.1 echo, pipelined, TLS 1.3 echo and WebSocket echo benchmarks, 10,000 connections, 1 KiB payload, GitHub-hosted ubuntu-24.04 runners with 4 vCPUs (2 for server, 2 for client), single run each.
claimed_speedup: HTTP/1.1 echo: fib 194,671 TPS vs workflow (C++) 150,407 (1.29x, derived from page data), memory 32 MB vs 14 MB; WebSocket echo: fib 138,592 vs uws_events 129,363 (1.07x, derived); README says fib is 'level with or close to' C, C++ and Rust servers; TLS 1.3 echo 103,427 vs uSockets 103,972 (tie).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27, CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags='-s -w' (HttpArena Dockerfile); workflow and uSockets build flags not stated.
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-24.04 runner, 4 vCPUs (CPU model stated only for a different benchmark: AMD EPYC 9V74)
tradeoffs: Event-loop networking library for Go that keeps the net/http handler model; no LICENSE file found in the repo, so reference only; uses far more memory than workflow (32 MB vs 14 MB) and TLS 1.3 pipelining uses 180 MB vs 51 MB for uSockets.
caveats: First-party single runs on noisy shared runners (the README says read differences of a few percent as ties). It loses to axum on HTTP/1 echo (236,244 vs 194,671), to uSockets and fnet/uws on WebSocket and TLS pipelining, and the workflow pipeline row is missing. In HttpArena it is slightly behind nginx at baseline-4096 (3,164,504 vs 3,284,513) but far ahead on h2c (12,891,491 at 256 connections vs nginx 2,456,329), where nginx is the only C server compared.
found_via: HttpArena results listing (fib.json, frameworks/fib/meta.json) led to the lesismal/fib README
why_faster: A few event loops wait for I/O readiness and a shared worker pool does the work, so an idle connection costs no goroutine; pipelined requests are batched (README).

name: Go net/http vs nginx on localhost (yosssi gist)
baseline: nginx (C); version and configuration not shown
workload: wrk -t12 -c400 -d2s against 127.0.0.1 for nginx and for Go net/http servers (empty handler, 'Hello' handler and three static-file variants).
claimed_speedup: nginx 31,780.82 req/s (avg latency 7.71 ms); Go empty handler with GOMAXPROCS=2 62,314.54 req/s (3.79 ms), about 1.96x (derived from page data); Go file server that copies with io.Copy 59,517.07 req/s (5.01 ms), about 1.87x (derived from page data). Other Go file-serving variants are slower than nginx: http.FileServer 16,088.43 req/s and http.ServeContent 25,581.43 req/s.
tradeoffs: Go runtime and GC; no TLS, keep-alive tuning or real file workload is exercised.
caveats: Weak, informal result. Runs last only 2 seconds, the load generator and servers share one machine (the author's home-directory paths and a 'mac:~' prompt in the gist suggest macOS), and Go and nginx versions, nginx configuration and the served content are not given. Every run shows socket errors (connect 155, timeouts 66). The empty-handler and Hello rows do not serve files, so they are not like-for-like with nginx; only the file-server rows are, and two of the three are slower than nginx. Two of the Go sections show identical code and one comment points out they look identical. Gist has no licence, so the code is reference only. Tier C: numbers without methodology.
found_via: WebSearch (github.com only): '"faster than nginx" OR "outperforms nginx" ... requests/sec README' surfaced the gist 'Go networking performance vs Nginx'; gist opened with WebFetch

name: ioxide
baseline: nginx 1.31.4 (C) and h2o (C) in the HttpArena suite; also libreactorng and libioma (C, io_uring), mongoose (C) and agensio (C++)
workload: HttpArena baseline (mixed GET/POST with query parsing, 4096 connections), pipelined and HTTP/2 profiles for a hand-written HTTP/1.1 handler on ioxide, a shared-nothing io_uring runtime for .NET (one ring per reactor thread, raw syscalls without liburing).
claimed_speedup: baseline-4096: 4,111,381 req/s vs nginx 3,284,513 (1.25x, derived from page data), h2o 3,641,609 (1.13x), mongoose 3,707,598 (1.11x), agensio 3,558,559 (1.16x). pipelined-4096: 53,376,982 vs nginx 4,037,345 and libreactorng 43,424,448. baseline-h2-1024: 12,235,767 vs nginx 3,320,285 (3.7x).
compiler_and_flags: .NET SDK 11.0.100-preview.7, dotnet publish -c Release (HttpArena frameworks/ioxide/Dockerfile); nginx -O3 -march=native.
hardware: HttpArena dedicated 64-core machine, containers per entry (README says '64-core dedicated hardware'; CPU model, RAM, NIC and kernel not stated)
tradeoffs: Linux-only (io_uring, seccomp must be unconfined), needs a preview .NET 11 runtime; HTTP/3 uses ngtcp2/nghttp3 and TLS uses OpenSSL (C libraries).
caveats: The ioxide repo is owned by the same GitHub account as the HttpArena suite (MDA2AV), so tier is C rather than B even though every entry runs through one public harness. The ioxide Dockerfile notes that moving from .NET 11 preview.6 to preview.7 took baseline-4096 from 4.11M to 3.90M with no change to the entry, so the saved figure depends on the runtime preview. It is behind libreactorng (4,377,377) and libioma (4,255,834), both C, at baseline-4096, behind nginx at limited-conn-4096 (2,543,314 vs 2,626,297), and behind h2o at baseline-h2-1024 (15,633,023). The repo README gives no throughput numbers against C servers. Results JSON files are undated and the suite is rerun by its maintainers; competitor rows (nginx, h2o, mongoose, libreactorng, libioma, drogon, cutelyst, hical, agensio) are read from sibling JSON files in the same directory, entries are minimal hand-written handlers (nginx is a custom C handler module), and the baseline-4096 profile mixes GET and POST with query parsing, not static files. CPU model not stated, so not tier A.
found_via: WebSearch 'comparative performance study web frameworks Rust actix-web Go Java Spring C++ Drogon' led to the-benchmarker/web-frameworks; HttpArena (github.com/MDA2AV/HttpArena) found by following the TechEmpower-style suites; per-entry JSON in site/data/results opened via raw.githubusercontent.com
why_faster: One io_uring ring per reactor thread, multishot accept and recv into provided buffer rings, inline continuations, no liburing (engine description in HttpArena meta.json); nginx in the same suite uses epoll.

name: kawipiko
baseline: NGINX (distribution package; configuration in the kawipiko examples/nginx folder), also darkhttpd
workload: Static 'Hello World!' file served from a CDB archive held in memory (kawipiko) or from tmpfs (NGINX), wrk over loopback with keep-alive, 512 to 16384 connections; plus a 250k-file OpenStreetMap tile set at 16384 connections.
claimed_speedup: 512 connections, 2 server threads: kawipiko 106,698.89 req/s vs NGINX 79,816.08 (1.34x, derived from page data); 2048 connections: 100,296.65 vs 78,211.46; 4096: 95,628.34 vs 75,970.82; 16384: 53,548.52 vs 43,909.67. Tile benchmark (i7 4770, 8 threads, 16384 connections): kawipiko 238,499.86 req/s vs NGINX 188,255.32 (1.27x, derived), with ~25% more requests/s, ~29% lower average latency and ~25% less CPU per request stated by the author.
compiler_and_flags: Go build of kawipiko (version and flags not stated); NGINX from distribution packages (version and build flags not stated); server run with --archive-inmem, --security-headers-disable and --timeout-disable.
hardware: Laptop with Intel Core i7 3667U (2 physical cores, 4 threads), 8 GiB RAM for the Hello World runs; desktop Intel Core i7 4770 (4 cores, 8 threads), 32 GiB for the tile run; wrk and server pinned to separate physical cores, tmpfs.
tradeoffs: Serves only a prebuilt CDB archive, so content changes need a rebuild; HTTP/2 is about 6 times slower than its HTTP/1 path (Go net/http), where the author says NGINX is much better; kawipiko used about 1 GiB RAM in the tile run while NGINX used the least; AGPL licence.
caveats: First-party; the per-connection rows are marked 'Last updated in August 2018' and the summary 'December 2021', measured on 2013-era CPUs (i7 3667U, i7 4770), the author says the current version is at least 10% more efficient. NGINX is a distro package with an author-tuned config; timeouts and security headers are disabled in the kawipiko run (author says timeouts cost 10-15%). Socket errors and timeouts appear in the 2048 and 16384 connection rows for both servers. The author states the real advantage over NGINX is deployment simplicity, not raw speed, and calls the result 'at least on-par'.
found_via: WebSearch 'static file web server written in Rust OR Zig OR Go "faster than nginx" benchmark wrk requests/sec README comparison h2o lwan' (github.com, gitlab.com, codeberg.org filter)
why_faster: Content pre-indexed in a CDB archive held in memory with a compact lookup (no per-request file system calls), on Go fasthttp; the README says the advantage grows for many small files accessed in random patterns.

name: linkerd2-proxy (Rust) vs Envoy as service-mesh sidecars
baseline: Envoy (C++), as the Istio sidecar proxy
workload: Linkerd versus Istio service-mesh benchmark on the Kinvolk service-mesh-benchmark harness (wrk2 load against emojivoto instances, 500 to 5000 RPS steps, Equinix Metal cluster); per-proxy memory, CPU and added latency.
claimed_speedup: From search snippets only (pages not opened): at 4000 RPS Linkerd proxies held about 14-15 MB of memory against 135-175 MB for Envoy, and about 15 CPU-ms against 22-156 CPU-ms per instance; a later Buoyant run (Linkerd 2.10.2 vs Istio 1.10.0) reported Istio adding 36% more median latency and 438% more maximum latency at the highest load, with Envoy proxies using about 8x the memory and CPU of Linkerd's Rust proxies.
hardware: Equinix Metal (per harness README, machine type not stated on the opened page)
stars_or_usage: about 2.1k stars; data plane of the Linkerd service mesh
tradeoffs: Purpose-built for Linkerd (mTLS, retries, load balancing for sidecar use), not a general reverse proxy; far smaller feature surface than Envoy.
caveats: Snippet only: linkerd.io, buoyant.io and the CNCF mirror are unreachable here (DNS block), so none of the numbers were read on their page; the opened pages carry no results. The linkerd2-proxy README has no benchmark, and the harness repo kinvolk/service-mesh-benchmark (Apache-2.0, archived 2024-02-06, 142 stars, wrk2 at 120 s and 3000 RPS by default, 500-5000 RPS steps) lists no results. The comparison is Linkerd versus Istio, so the Envoy side reflects Istio's sidecar configuration and feature set, and the vendor (Buoyant) has a commercial stake; the authors themselves called it not an entirely fair comparison. The language is not isolated from the design difference. Tier C at best until a page with numbers is opened.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Linkerd2-proxy Rust vs Envoy C++ service mesh benchmark latency CPU memory Kinvolk' (snippets from Buoyant and Linkerd posts); repo and harness opened on github.com.
why_faster: Purpose-built minimal sidecar proxy in Rust versus the general-purpose Envoy (design scope, per the vendor); the language effect is not isolated.

name: monolake
baseline: nginx 1.24.0 (C); build flags not stated
workload: HTTP and HTTPS proxy/serving throughput of the Monolake reference proxy (Rust on the io_uring-based monoio runtime) against nginx, measured as requests per second versus response body size (512 B to 64 KiB) and versus worker threads (1 to 16); load generator, nginx configuration and backend setup are not stated.
claimed_speedup: No numbers in the text; four chart images only. Approximate values read from the charts (not stated by the project). HTTPS vs worker threads: 16 threads about 526k req/s vs nginx about 450k (about 1.17x), 8 threads about 359k vs about 334k (about 1.07x). HTTPS vs body size: 512 B about 152k vs about 128k (about 1.19x), 4096 B about 124k vs about 108k (about 1.15x), roughly equal at 8192 B, then nginx ahead at 16384 B (about 55k vs about 59k) and 65536 B (about 20k vs about 23k). Plain HTTP: nginx ahead everywhere, 16 threads about 707k vs about 688k (monolake about 0.97x), 512 B about 186k vs about 168k (monolake about 0.91x).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for Monolake or nginx; Monolake needs Rust nightly and Linux 5.1+ for io_uring (docs).
hardware: AWS c6a.8xlarge, AMD EPYC 7R13, 16 cores / 32 threads, 64 GB RAM, Linux 6.1.94-99.176.amzn2023.x86_64 (Amazon Linux 2023.5.20240805), nginx 1.24.0 (README Performance section)
stars_or_usage: 66 stars; README says it was deployed in production at ByteDance
tradeoffs: Archived by the owner on 2025-08-29 and marked no longer recommended for use; needs Rust nightly and Linux io_uring (falls back to epoll elsewhere); HTTP/Thrift proxy framework rather than a general web server.
caveats: First-party charts with no tabulated numbers, so values here are eyeballed from PNGs. The win is confined to HTTPS with small bodies (and more worker threads); plain HTTP and large HTTPS bodies favour nginx. The nginx build and configuration (workers, logging, TLS library), the workload (static body or proxied backend) and the load generator are not stated, and the TLS stack on each side is unknown. Repository is archived. Tier C: first-party, partial methodology.
found_via: WebSearch 'monolake Rust proxy benchmark vs Nginx throughput cloudwego' surfaced the project; github.com/cloudwego/monolake README Performance section and its four chart PNGs (raw.githubusercontent.com .github/images) opened
why_faster: Thread-per-core io_uring runtime (monoio) with no work stealing, versus nginx's epoll workers; the README gives no explicit explanation for the HTTPS win.

name: Orion Proxy
baseline: Envoy Proxy (C++)
workload: HTTP reverse proxy to an nginx upstream, wrk at 2048 and 16384 connections, 1 to 48 cores assigned to the proxy.
claimed_speedup: README: '2x-4x better throughput and latency than Envoy Proxy'. Chart labels in docs/pics/performance/baseline/wrk-reqsec.png, requests/s Orion vs Envoy: 2048 connections, 1 core 46,593 vs 12,819, 48 cores 1,881,522 vs 310,231 (6.1x, derived from page data); 16384 connections, 1 core 38,573 vs 17,059, 48 cores 1,410,611 vs 514,254 (2.7x, derived).
hardware: Two-host testbed: DUT proxy host and tester host with wrk on NUMA 0 and nginx upstream on NUMA 1, 25 Gbps Mellanox and Intel NICs, IRQ affinity tuned (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Envoy xDS-compatible Rust proxy aiming at a drop-in replacement for common use cases only; not the full Envoy filter set.
caveats: First-party; the numbers exist only as chart images (read from the PNG labels), the performance page also names 'Ng-proxy' and nginx as compared proxies but only Orion and Envoy appear in the chart read. Envoy version, build and config, Orion build flags and CPU model are not stated, so tier C. The stated 2x-4x is lower than the 6x seen in the 2048-connection chart at 48 cores.
found_via: WebSearch 'Monolake Rust proxy benchmark vs Nginx Envoy throughput latency' returned the kmesh-net community issue about Orion
why_faster: README credits Rust's zero-cost abstractions and memory safety guarantees (no profiling or mechanism analysis is given).

name: routez
baseline: nginx 1.30.5 (C) and HAProxy 3.2.23 (C)
workload: nginx-style edge server in Zig 0.17 measured with wrk, keep-alive, 256 connections, 3 workers each, median of 3 x 10 s runs, on Docker Desktop on an Apple M-series Mac (10 cores).
claimed_speedup: requests/s routez vs nginx: fixed response 627k vs 529k (1.19x, derived from page data), reverse proxy to keep-alive upstream 262k vs 208k (1.26x), TLS fixed response 582k vs 324k (1.8x), TLS 10 KB static file 208k vs 152k (1.4x), TLS new connection per request 17k vs 13k; p99 at a held 208k req/s fixed response 3.6 ms vs nginx 21.2 ms.
compiler_and_flags: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast; nginx build flags not stated (nginx given open_file_cache, off by default)
hardware: Apple M-series Mac, 10 cores, Docker Desktop VM (the author writes 'a VM is not a benchmark machine'), 20 Sep 2026
tradeoffs: Pure Zig edge server with HTTP/1.1, HTTP/3, TLS 1.3, ACME, reverse proxy and load balancing; no license file found, so reference only.
caveats: The author's own table is mixed: 10 KB static file 308k vs nginx 312k (a tie); full RSA-2048 TLS handshakes 1.0k/s vs nginx 3.6k/s; HTTP/3 static file 94k/s vs 247k/s; p99 at a held rate proxied 4.30 ms vs HAProxy 1.79 ms. Benchmark code is in the repo (bench/run.sh) but the run is on a macOS VM with a vague CPU, a single run set, and nginx's build is not given, so tier C.
found_via: WebSearch '"faster than nginx" Rust OR Zig OR Go reverse proxy web server benchmark wrk results README' (github.com filter)
why_faster: Worker threads with SO_REUSEPORT on libxev, an open-file cache and sendfile for plain-HTTP static files (README feature list); no profile attribution for the wins.

name: rproxy
baseline: nginx as a reverse proxy (version and config not stated); HAProxy 2.8.5 (vendored build) as a second row
workload: HTTP/1.1 reverse proxy in front of an nginx backend answering '200 OK' with a 2-byte body, wrk -t4 -c100 -d10s keep-alive, two proxy workers each for rproxy and nginx on two pinned cores, loopback.
claimed_speedup: August run: rproxy 323,035 req/s (352 us avg) vs nginx reverse proxy 282,032 (400 us) = 1.15x and HAProxy 266,603 (395 us); June run (median of 3, bare metal): rproxy 189,810 (557 us) vs nginx 153,484 (662 us) = 1.24x. Backend ceiling without a proxy 632,175 (August) / 362,163 (June).
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release (no other flags stated); monoio with io_uring; nginx build and flags not stated.
hardware: i5-12450H (12 logical cores); wrk on cores 4-7, backend nginx on cores 0-1, proxy on cores 2-3
tradeoffs: Not a general reverse proxy: the author positions it as a filtering layer (JWT, rate limiting, ACL and canonicalization checks) behind nginx; Linux with io_uring (kernel 5.6+); rate limit and cache state are per worker; TLS rate 134,168 req/s vs ceiling 629,459.
caveats: First-party numbers with no run date inside the README (the benchmark file bench/BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md was not opened). The README is internally inconsistent about HAProxy: a measured row is shown, then a later section says 'HAProxy was not measured on the current rig' and no comparison is claimed. The two runs report different ceilings (362k vs 632k) without explanation. Small keep-alive body, same box, no TLS; larger bodies, no keep-alive or TLS may differ. No LICENSE file at the repo root, so reference. Repo has 2 commits and no stars. nginx version and config are not stated.
found_via: WebSearch 'Rust OR Go reverse proxy benchmark vs nginx HAProxy Envoy requests per second github README results wrk' (github.com filter)
why_faster: Prefork thread-per-core monoio workers on io_uring with a zero-allocation hot path (README architecture section).

name: Spire
baseline: HAProxy 2.7.3 (C) and Envoy 1.22.8 (C++) reverse proxies; nginx 1.23.3 in the same table is faster than Spire
workload: hey -n 100000 -c 250 GET through each reverse proxy to one backend, docker-compose, proxy and backend limited to 4 CPU cores and 8 GB memory; based on the public NickMRamirez/Proxy-Benchmarks harness.
claimed_speedup: Spire 114,512 req/s (avg 2.2 ms, p99 11.8 ms) vs HAProxy 85,406 (1.34x, derived from page data), Envoy 48,040 (2.38x), Traefik 59,487 (1.93x), Caddy 13,168 (8.70x); but nginx 1.23.3 reached 148,677 req/s, so Spire is 0.77x of nginx (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated; proxies run as Docker images in docker-compose (versions listed: HAProxy 2.7.3, Envoy 1.22.8, Traefik 2.9.8, NGINX 1.23.3, Caddy 2.6.4); Spire built with cargo build --release per README
hardware: 13th Gen Intel Core i5-13600K PC, 32 GB RAM (benchmarks.md); services limited to 4 cores and 8 GB
tradeoffs: Rust reverse proxy and gateway on Tokio and Hyper (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC, TCP/TLS) with rate limiting, circuit breaking, ACME and hot reload; about 7 MB binary and 4 MB start-up memory per README.
caveats: Not faster than nginx in its own table (114,512 vs 148,677 req/s, p99 11.8 ms vs 4.9 ms); the claim holds only against HAProxy, Envoy, Traefik and Caddy. Single hey run of 100,000 requests lasting about 1 s per proxy, load generator on the same PC, old HAProxy 2.7.3 and Envoy 1.22.8 releases, default or unstated proxy configs, and the README headline 'Exceptional Performance' is not backed by a win over nginx. Flags are not stated, so it cannot be tier A.
found_via: WebSearch 'Rust OR Go reverse proxy load balancer github benchmark outperforms nginx and HAProxy requests per second README' and github.com/topics/reverse-proxy?l=rust; README and benchmarks.md opened
why_faster: README attributes it to the Tokio async runtime and the Hyper HTTP library; no mechanism analysis is given.

name: statico
baseline: nginx (static in-memory 'return' response)
workload: Synthetic static in-memory HTTP response served to 1024 connections at 1, 2 and 4 server threads, comparing statico runtimes with nginx, HAProxy, Go net/http, fasthttp, Axum and actix-web.
claimed_speedup: requests/s, 1 / 4 threads: statico (tokio) 399,025 / 1,071,433 vs nginx (return) 286,960 / 832,082 (1.39x / 1.29x, derived from page data); statico (monoio) 656,517 / 1,436,420 (2.29x / 1.73x, derived); README text says standard statico is about 40% faster single-threaded.
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release (feature flags per runtime); nginx build and flags not stated.
tradeoffs: Designed strictly for benchmarking: returns a fixed response from memory, no routing, no logging; Linux-only io_uring runtimes.
caveats: First-party, no CPU model, load generator or nginx configuration published, so tier C. The README's own observations list monoio at 1.36M req/s at four threads while its table gives 1,436,420. Actix-web (798,809) is slower than nginx (832,082) at four threads in the same table, and the README does not say whether nginx used its tuned worker settings.
found_via: WebSearch 'paper performance evaluation HTTP server written in Rust outperforms nginx C requests per second arXiv' returned docs.rs statico pages; repo from crates.io API (repository field)
why_faster: Pre-built responses held in memory, HTTP pipelining, thread-per-core io_uring runtimes (tokio-uring, monoio, glommio, compio) with CPU pinning for glommio and compio (README).

name: swerver
baseline: nginx (OpenResty alpine image with a tuned nginx.conf)
workload: swerver-benchmarks: k6 scenarios against minimal endpoints (/health, /echo, /blob) in Docker with 2 CPUs and 512 MB per container, swerver vs nginx, actix, http-zig and APISIX.
claimed_speedup: GET /health, 100 VUs, 30 s: swerver 147,435 req/s vs nginx 118,061 (1.25x, derived from page data), actix 133,691; no keep-alive connections/s 90,657 vs nginx 19,206 (4.7x); rapid-fire 143,437 vs nginx 125,346; error handling 114,455 vs nginx 80,053; TLS /health h2 161,781 vs nginx 107,741.
compiler_and_flags: swerver: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast (swerver README); nginx: openresty/openresty:alpine image, flags not stated
hardware: Docker Desktop on macOS Apple Silicon, 2 CPU cores and 512 MB per container, April 2026 (exact chip not stated)
tradeoffs: Alpha release; library API will change; HTTP/3 first version runs at 16.5K req/s.
caveats: First-party benchmark by the swerver author. Hot endpoints are served from a per-second-refreshed pre-encoded response cache that skips router, middleware and encoder, while nginx answers /echo through content_by_lua and /health with 'return 200'. Docker Desktop macOS VM, seccomp unconfined so io_uring is used. Results are mixed: mixed workload 36,929 vs nginx 36,969 (tie), /echo latency scenario nginx 8,659 vs swerver 8,517, and actix-web is ahead of swerver on TLS throughput (171,726 vs 161,781). Another Zig server (http-zig) is far behind nginx on several rows.
found_via: WebSearch '"faster than nginx" Rust OR Zig OR Go reverse proxy web server benchmark wrk results README' (github.com filter)
why_faster: io_uring backend plus a pre-encoded response cache for hot endpoints that skips the router, middleware and response encoder (swerver-benchmarks README).

name: Traefik (Go reverse proxy; TLS latency vs Nginx and HAProxy)
baseline: Nginx 1.28.3 (C) and HAProxy 3.3.6 (C) in Docker; proxy configs live in configs/{nginx,caddy,traefik,haproxy}/ and were not displayed
workload: Fixed-rate load of 5,000 req/s for 20 s with Vegeta (64 connections, about 20 KB JSON payload, 5 s warmup, shuffled order) through each proxy to a backend, over plain HTTP/1.1, HTTPS/1.1 and HTTPS/2.
claimed_speedup: README results (approximate values, all four at 100% success): HTTPS/1.1 Traefik mean about 0.48 ms and P99 about 1.47 ms, Nginx P99 about 24 ms; HTTPS/2 Traefik mean about 0.46 ms and P99 about 1.37 ms, HAProxy P99 about 1.79 ms. Plain HTTP/1.1: all four within about 5%, Caddy and HAProxy lowest mean (about 0.41 ms), HAProxy lowest P99 (about 1.09 ms). Per-proxy tables for every scenario are not published.
compiler_and_flags: Official container images: Nginx 1.28.3, Caddy 2.11.2, Traefik 3.6.13, HAProxy 3.3.6; Vegeta v12.13.0; no compiler flags (prebuilt images)
hardware: Not stated (Docker on the author's machine; an optional restricted run limits each proxy to 2 CPU cores and 4 GB RAM)
tradeoffs: The benchmark records latency percentiles and success rate only; CPU and memory use are not reported. The author states that Nginx wins plaintext throughput and recommends running the suite on one's own hardware.
caveats: Benchmark repo is a third-party suite but a 0-star personal repo that the owner archived on 2026-07-17, with no hardware stated and only approximate best-per-scenario values in the README. It is a fixed-rate latency test at 5,000 req/s, not a saturation throughput test. The Nginx TLS P99 of about 24 ms probably reflects configuration (session cache, buffer sizes) rather than the language gap, and the configs were not read; the README itself says 'in this environment'. No HTTP/1.1 win: the author calls plain HTTP 'extremely tight' and credits Nginx with plaintext throughput. Tier C: partial methodology, hardware missing.
found_via: WebSearch (github.com only): '"faster than nginx" OR "outperforms nginx" ... web server proxy written in Rust Go Zig Java requests/sec README' surfaced fabianwimberger/reverse-proxy-benchmark; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com, traefik/traefik commits page opened for the date

name: wut-server
baseline: nginx (C; own build with all optimization options, LTO, static OpenSSL, ngx_headers_more; 1 worker, 1024 worker connections, HTTP/2, TLS 1.3 only)
workload: wrk against a single endpoint that returns the caller's IP address: 10 s, 6 threads, 1000 connections (inferred from the output header), nginx on port 443 versus wut-server on port 11313 of the same host.
claimed_speedup: 38,110.60 requests/s (382,057 requests in 10 s) vs nginx 25,650.31 (257,322), about 49% more per the page (1.49x, derived from page data); transfer 3.27 MB/s vs 2.79 MB/s; max latency 279.57 ms vs 520.46 ms; nginx had connect 95 and read 17 socket errors.
compiler_and_flags: Rust build flags not stated; nginx build described above, version not stated.
hardware: Server: single-core AMD EPYC 7302P, 1 GB ECC RAM, 1 Gbit/s uplink; client: AMD Ryzen 5600, 32 GB ECC RAM, 250 Mbit/s uplink; OS not stated; network benchmark, not loopback.
tradeoffs: Single-purpose server that returns the caller's public IP over HTTP and HTTP/2; not a general web server.
caveats: First-party single run with no variance, no wrk command line and no versions. Average latency is higher for wut-server (45.00 ms vs 28.07 ms). The two servers listen on different ports and it is not stated whether wut-server terminates TLS on port 11313, so TLS work may differ; the run is over the network with a 250 Mbit/s client uplink and nginx shows socket errors, so the nginx side may be limited by the path rather than the server. The page compares only against nginx and the benchmark harness is not in the repo.
